utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you understand that you are still under the oath that you took when you began your testimony to tell the truth, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the end of yesterday's hearing, Mr. Tadic, we were discussing your military history in 1993. You gave evidence concerning occasions when you were arrested and there was an enforced mobilization at Gradacac. I would like you now to look at a number of documents, the first of which I produce dated 9th June 1993. If this could be provided to the Registry for identification purposes as D96 with translations? Your Honour, these documents were provided to the Prosecution during the video link stage of the trial. It seems from our information that the witness to replace Budimir, Aleksic will not be available to testify. I have spoken to Mr. Niemann about this matter this morning and he has agreed that it is appropriate these documents come in through the accused, although they are not his documents and there will be no objection to their admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Then there will be no objection raised then by the Prosecution as to any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am very grateful. There is a full set here for your Honours and if I can hand those in to you?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 96 then will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, if the remaining pages are also put before the witness as part of 96, it will be an easier and quicker way to proceed. [To the witness]: If you can keep them in the order that has been provided, Mr. Tadic? Beneath each Serbo-Croat document is a document that has been translated in English. Perhaps if we can look at the document dated 9th June 1993? Just looking at this document, it indicates that, indeed, you were arrested or an order was given to a Sergeant Desimir Grujicic on 9th June 1993 relating to Prijedor and Pecani. The patrol assignment was the apprehension of the conscript Dusko Tadic and his remand to command post, Slatina, pursuant to the order of seizure of 8th June 1993. I think you told us yesterday that Desimir was the man who arrested you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- the name is Grujicic. I do not think your pronunciation was correct -- it was Grujicic -- and he was there every time they tried to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. If we could then move to the next document beneath that which is headed: "Patrol leader report on the completed assignment", it indicates there that you were apprehended and remanded to South Slatina on 9th June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this handwriting. It is very familiar to me because at the time when I was arrested, Desimir showed me the arrest warrant which was in similar handwriting, and also a fax which he had received from Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the information of the Court, the official note beneath that is a note that was put on the document later by a Judge in Banja Luka and is not part of the original document, but was used at a time when it was felt that that would be a means of providing the evidence before the Court. If we look then to the next document which is dated 21st July '93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If only I could say I remember this was June 9 of '93. At that time it was the first time that I was arrested in a legal way by the military police. I remember that I was then arrested in my office, at my workplace, in Kozarac. They arrested me several times, but this time on that day they took me to the front and I returned the same day. I think it was -- I spent the night there, I think it was Friday, and then I went back and I was arrested again on the next day, and returned to the front. It was always Desimir who did this and his patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think that we saw yesterday your mobilization, your military book which showed your mobilization being stamped in the book for 10th June '93 which would have been the day after the arrest and the day after those documents that we have just looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you will allow me to tell it? On the 9th June of '93, I was arrested in Kozarac, and then I was taken in a van to Prijedor, to the headquarters of -- it was the fire station. I know it was their headquarters. Then in the same van I was taken to the front, and on the same day I escaped. Desimir himself said that it was not done to any of the Secretaries of the Local Commune, and he said that the warrant is a warrant and he had to do what it said. Indeed, in the warrant it said that I should be remanded for an interview. That evening I managed to get back. I came back very late to Pecani. I remembered spending the night there and in the morning when my wife and I went for coffee, the same group, actually a little bigger group, waited for me. They were in front of the building and I said, "At least allow me to have coffee". They said, "No, no, we have to go". Desimir showed me the fax and said, "We were looking for you all night", and many people did not know where to look for me, the military. As far as the military book is concerned, they allowed me to go back to the apartment, get the documents concerning my military and my work, my employment, and those documents always were the evidence against the impropriety, the illegality, of their actions. So I turned all my documents over to my wife, the military book and the employment decision, and I told her to get in touch with our brother immediately, to go to the office of the Defence because I was not sure that things were going to come out right. On several occasions I was told that there was no chance of me staying in Prijedor. They would do anything to destroy me. So I was quite afraid. I did not understand all the reasons, only later did I understand why this was being done. But, all in all, when I came back home the next time, my wife, that is what she told me later. She went with my brother to the municipal office and they would not talk to them there. She went to Miskovic, Simo Miskovic. Apparently, they called the National Defence and they paid a visit there and again they achieved nothing. So they were running in a circle. Generally, they did not even know where I was. At the time they did not know where I had gone to. My brother, when I was taken away, did not know where I went. They would not tell him and later he found somebody, and they found out that I was in Gradacac and there were many places where the military was located. This is the first time at the front that I saw that military book. Mile Cavic who was the company Commander gave me this book. I had left it with my wife and I got it back in Gradacac. My wife told me that Mr. Budimir told her, "Everything is going to be resolved, give me the book", and that was a mistake because they stamped it and then it was definitive, the proof that I was tied to this military unit. You could not get another stamp unless you got it from the highest authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we understand this point. What I want to do is just to put these records in before the Court at this stage. We understand the purpose of your testimony on this matter. If we just look at the next document dated 21st July '93, and it is patrol sheet 019/-95? Again it refers to Sergeant Desimir Grujicic and states on 21st July 1993 they were ordered to patrol facilities and routes indicated in the Prijedor region. Again the purpose was the apprehension of the conscript Dusko Tadic and remand to the Unit's deployment area pursuant to the order of the Battalion Commander of 19th July 1993. That is the order they got, but if we look at the next document we indicated we can see how it impacted upon you, because it states that you were apprehended on 21st July 1993. Is that right, that on 21st July 1993 that was another occasion as part of your enforced mobilization that they had arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see there the region to be searched around Kozarac and Prijedor. I would always go to my workplace in Kozarac. When I spoke to the Secretary in the municipality, who was in charge of all the Secretaries of the Local Commune, he said, "You have to report there in the specific time of the day", but it was a circle because whenever I would show up at work I was afraid that I may be arrested, and often times it did happen that I was arrested. So I wanted to move somewhere else, to another -- in the school there were a lot of rooms. I was persecuted. I was not aware of what was going on. Sometimes when I would come to Kozarac my neighbours would say, "The military police was looking for you". I was surprised because they could have found me, but often they were looking for me. This time I know that I was taken to Slatina in a luxury car. It was a zastava model 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the next document dated 9th August 1993, again we see a patrol sheet, again it is Sergeant Desimir Grujicic and we see the order for the apprehension of the conscript Dusko Tadic upon the orders of the Battalion Commander of 5th August 1993. That is the order. If we look at the next document beneath it we can see a note related to the completed assignment and, "The individual was taken into custody on the premises of the Fire Brigade in Prijedor, and after the interview with the personnel or personal officer, Gavrilovic, the individual escaped".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember this event very well. At the time my wife was already abroad in Germany, and I was in Prijedor by myself with my mother and I was living in an apartment above Jugo-Banka. I remember in the morning I went to find medicine for my mother, gangrene of a toe, and I saw the police van approaching. At first, I did not know who they were looking for. Then Desimir beckoned to me. I turned around and started to run, and he started running after me. I remember jumping over a fence, two fences, and he was jumping over after me. I came to a wall and he said, "Stop or I will shoot." I turned around and I really saw him. He was holding a gun. Maybe I would continue running ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Maybe I could stop you here. We do not need this detail as it is not that crucial for the case. The facts are spoken of within the documents and I do not think the Court would object if I interrupted you on that matter. If we look at the next document that is dated 30th August 1993, we again see the same order. Again it is Sergeant Desimir Grujicic and the order of 30th August 1993, "shall patrol the facilities, routes, areas indicated below, Prijedor, Pecani, Kozarac", and the assignment is to remand the conscript Dusko Tadic pursuant to an order of 28th August 1993. If we look at the last page, which is a final report, it says, on the completed assignment, but it says, "The conscript Dusko Tadic was not found at the indicated address or seen in the Prijedor or in Kozarac. He was sought at regular intervals and has not been found". What I would like to ask you about is this. That reviews those documents. You referred to your wife being in Germany during this period. Can you tell us why she left for Germany during this summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we were not clear about the main reasons were my arrest. We simply could not survive there any more together. At moments it seemed to us that it was because I got this cafe to use, and it was a Major of the army of Republika Srpska was behind it, but it was not the real reason. I took some confidence in thinking that was the only reason, but when I was taken to the fire station, when my wife had already gone abroad, it was then that I realised that the difference -- that the reasons were very different and after that interview at the fire station I fled and I never went back. I only once went back while I was in Banja Luka. It was at night. I visited friends in Prijedor, and I asked them what to do and they said it was best for me to leave and not to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did your wife leave the area to go to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She left after -- before this arrest on 9th August, and after my arrest of 21st July, somewhere in that period. I am not sure, but I know that I saw them off to Belgrade. I returned and I was arrested promptly. So that was the very end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to Germany as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Germany in November from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Between August and November where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Banja Luka, hiding at my brother's, and I was staying there during the day, but I was afraid that they would come and look for me there. So I was sleeping at his mother-in-law, at Milosa Duica Street, with Ljubo's son Nenad. He was keeping me company there, even though he was living with the brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was your reason then for going to Germany in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my arrest in the fire station, I knew that I could not survive in Prijedor. Major Gavrilovic, he is the one who interrogated me. It was not just an interview, it was not just an interview; it was an interrogation, and at that time I realised that I had to leave the Prijedor municipality as soon as possible and go as far as possible. I did not know that I would go to Germany. I did not want to stay in the Republika Srspka. Gavrilovic told me openly, he knew -- he had all the information about the brothers, "You are no warriors, you are no soldiers". He was mocking us. "They were good in karate but they do not fight". Now he had all the information. In general, he cited the reasons. I remember signing a few documents after the interrogation. At first, he said that he would take me to Radio Prijedor to publicly apologise to the Bosnian Serb Army because I had said that they were a private army. I showed him the document that I had work obligation. He said, "I will check it with Slavko Budimir", and he said, "Yes, this is a legal document, but we will revoke it today", and he said, "No, no, you will stay here", and then I was detained. There was a detention unit in the fire station, and he said, "You are going to sign that we are not a private army, that you will sign that you were a representative of Muslims". Then I remembered that it was during the period of time when I was taking part in the civic forum activities, and I told him that I was coming to Prijedor with a group of citizens that had nothing to do with any power or government. I was not connected to them. He said, "No, no, no. You negotiated on behalf of people who later turned against the Serb authorities", and I said that I would sign that I was a member of this delegation, but I did not know the background of all this. I could not have known. I did not know if there was somebody who wanted to manipulate me. He said, "It was only formal negotiations. You were really preparing for a war". So I said that I would sign. He said, "I will let you go if you sign". Then he said, "I cannot let you go, but if people from the military police let you, you can go to your mother's". I heard, overheard, when he gave the order for the van to be prepared and for me to be taken to the front. Somebody told me, "I did not know what is going on. I do not know where they are taking you, but you will be killed on the front". So, in August, the unit where I was was not on the front line. At that time I realised for the first time the seriousness of what was going on, and I told to a soldier, the last salary, the last money that I had, I gave to this Desimir so that I could be allowed to take medicine to my mother. I had about 50 Marks. I ran into the apartment, my mother's, grabbed all the documents that I had and fled towards Banja Luka. I went on foot to Petrov Gaj where I knew that the priest Majkic lived. So I stopped there for a coffee. A train arrived and that is how I got to Banja Luka. All in all, I went on foot. I did not use the same road. When I would hear vehicles, I would go into the fields. When I came to the priest, I know he was surprised at how I looked. I was filthy and sweaty. I did not tell him what had happened. I was embarrassed. I just told him that I was going to Banja Luka and I did not tell him what was going on. When I was in Banja Luka later, I called some of my friends and asked them what was going on. I had a telephone number of somebody in the military police, Riki Lekenic, and he told me not to go -- leave Banja Luka, that he would come to Banja Luka and tell me what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to Munich in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first went to Nuremberg and then my brother Mladen came to Nuremberg and took me to Munich.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you stay in the house of your brother Mladen in Munich?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the same apartment as he did for a certain period of time. It was a studio, and then I moved to a room which was part of his club, and that is where I lived. That is where I lived with my wife and my two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were in Munich is it right that you were arrested on 12th February 1994 by the German police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Subsequently, you were interviewed by investigators for the Prosecution Office of the Tribunal on 9th to 10th May 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And 21st to 22nd December 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I have to ask you. If you could remain there?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, may I ask the Court for the Court's indulgence for a brief recess? I was having a document attended to by the translation unit which, I think, will expedite matters considerably. It has not arrived and I will check on its progress.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you expect that you will have it or do you need a recess to check on its progress? Hopefully to check on its progress but also to have it, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have 10?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have to keep them satisfied. We try very hard. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In your testimony you spoke about the good people of Kozarac, predominantly Muslims. Those good people, at least most of them, are not there any more, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They were driven from their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably some of them were chased away and some left of their own will, but not all of them have been chased away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Many were rounded up and put into camps, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Many of the Muslims from Kozarac and from opstina Prijedor were rounded up by Serbian forces and put in camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take part in any of such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you were aware that that was happening in opstina Prijedor in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I first visited Kozarac I did not find my neighbours there. At that moment I did not know what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The religious buildings of the Muslim community were all destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my first visit I saw that some had been destroyed and later when I came back to work as the Secretary of the Local Commune, yes, it is true that all religious property in Kozarac was destroyed. Many of them were also destroyed in Prijedor although there was no war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time you left opstina Prijedor, about 90 per cent of the Muslim community of the entire opstina had been killed, forced out or thrown out, is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the percentage would be exactly. I did not have any conversations about that. I am not very well informed of the percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the vast majority of the Muslim community of opstina Prijedor forced out of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably some were forced and some left of their own will because they simply could not survive there any longer. There were several reasons, but many of Serbs also left the area. A great percentage left the area for different reasons, economic reasons, and simply because they did not want to take part in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslim community of opstina Prijedor was done under the direction of the authorities of the new opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was under their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those new authorities were comprised of persons who wanted and created a Srpski, Serbian opstina Prijedor and a Serbian Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intentions were not clear to me, the intentions of the new authorities, whether it was about creation of Republika Srpska within Bosnia or something else, I do not know. I was not aware of -- I did not know about the intentions of those authorities. They were not made public. You could only guess, assume, and I assumed that they themselves did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony on Friday, I believe, in response to a question from your attorney, that you did not conduct the plebiscite in 1991 on behalf of the SDS, because the plebescite was conducted through the Skupstina Opstine, through the elected local assembly, on behalf of the whole opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can the witness be presented with Exhibit 146, please? I am sorry, that may be the wrong number. Your Honour, the Court may know this Exhibit. It is the decision on the plebiscite which was displayed in Court on October 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How many hundreds of Exhibits do we have, 149? I do not know. I do not have the list of Exhibits before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it is 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is what I have it listed as well. May I see the Exhibit for the moment and make sure that we are talking about the same one? That is the correct number, thank you. Sir, this document, the decision on appointment of voting officials for the plebiscite, is headed as the "Instruction for the Plebiscite of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina", is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you look at the top of the page and see what that instruction indicates? Is that not pursuant to paragraph (2) under (4) of the instruction for the plebiscite of Serb people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an instruction, but this is not the instruction on the plebescite. Here it says, "pursuant to paragraph (2) under (4) instructions for the plebiscite", so it is based on the instruction, was this decision issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This particular decision? The appointment decision itself, although it cannot be seen on the monitor at the moment, is written in Cyrillic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is a stamp at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What does that stamp say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, municipal board, Prijedor".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated in your testimony that the plebiscite itself was conducted in the churchyard of the Serbian Orthodox church because, you said, you did not want the plebiscite conducted in a private home and "there were no other communal objects". In fact, there were a variety of communal objects and buildings in Kozarac, but the Orthodox church was the only exclusively Serbian communal object, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Orthodox church in Kozarac is over 120 years old, and all people visited, not only the church but also the churchyard, Muslims, Croats and others. I remember. I grew up there. We used to play football there. We spent a lot of time there in the churchyard, not only of the Orthodox church, but of the mosque as well -- me and my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the mosque was a communal object or building, the Mjesna Zajednica was a communal building, the post office was a communal building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the Serbian Orthodox church was the only Serbian communal building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was the main board of the SDS which entrusted you with the responsibility to conduct the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not the main board, the municipal committee. At that time in the municipality of Prijedor there was a government which did not belong to any party, and the municipal committee reached a decision, issued instructions, as to the way the plebiscite should be conducted. The municipal committee was not composed only of members of the SDS. I do not even know if there were any members of the SDS there. Maybe, I know that there was a Croat was a member of that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before you left Prijedor, you prepared a report to the SDS about your work from 1990 to 1993, is that right? We have seen that document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 8th, 8th August, I prepared that document in Kozarac and it was composed on the basis of various sources, sources of information, and various reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You sent that report to a number of different places and persons. For example, you sent it to the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the intention to do so, but I simply had no time to do it. I sent the document on the same day, that is, on 8th August. I took it personally to the office in the town hall in Prijedor. I had one copy with myself, and that copy was sent by me at the end of August through Rajko Lekenic to Prijedor to the main board of the Serbian Democratic Party. So one copy should be with the SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also prepared that work report to be sent to the President of the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was -- there were not many preparations there. I just did it within 20 minutes. I was sitting in the office in Kozarac. I was afraid that I would be arrested. So I wrote it on the basis of what I had seen in the office in Kozarac and on the basis of some reports that I had there, on the basis of my recollection. So I managed to compose it and I managed to write it on a typewriter although I had never used a typewriter before. So I managed to do it very quickly and to hand it over there, but I do not think it was really sent anywhere. As far as I know, I personally handed it over in the town hall in Prijedor and Rajko Lekenic took it from Banja Luka to the main board of the SDS in Prijedor, and I do not think that anything was sent to any other address. There is another copy of that report which is with me, and I took it with myself to Belgrade and then to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Copies were intended, however, whether they managed to get there or not, to go to, among others, the President of the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS? You typed that yourself, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But they were intended for many other addresses as well. For example, Commission for the Security and Co-operation in Europe, the Red Cross of Yugoslavia, to many other organisations that I had visited. I showed that document to the representative of the United Nations in Belgrade, because in October I had talks with them. They received me and I showed that document to them. They saw it and we talked, and then they referred me to the Federal Executive Council and they told me that I should try to exercise my rights there and ask about what had been happening to me in Prijedor municipality. I also visited the International Red Cross which had its seat in Sremska Mitrovica at that time. I also went to the seat of the UNHCR in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think you have answered the question that was asked. In that report you said that in November 1991 the main board of the SDS in Prijedor municipality entrusted you with the task of organising the plebiscite for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it says so exactly, but I probably thought that it was so. It should not -- it is not necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May the witness also be shown Exhibit 97, I believe? May the English be placed on the monitor, please? Can you bring that down just a little bit? No, I am sorry about the confusion. We want the first page of that document which is the ballot paper. This document depicts the two ballots which were used for the plebiscite, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose so. It is not very legible, but I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those ballots are headed "The Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The plebiscite was important to the SDS, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it not a sign of loyalty to the Serbian cause to vote in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it not true that Serbs were denounced as disloyal for failing to vote in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess you could say so, but it was not a general attitude at that time. It was not publicly said that way. It was believed that it was perfectly normal and that it is the duty of citizens to vote at the plebiscite, that it was their civic duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, did you not denounce Serbs as disloyal for failing to vote in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that they are people who could not be trusted, loyal or not loyal. I do not know whether someone should be loyal to me. Maybe in a later period ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just as you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- certain things were made clear, so I could have an impression that those were the people who were not aware of their own desires, who did not have any specific attitudes about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the plebiscite. Just like many other people at that time, we, simple people, ordinary people, did not know much about things at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you not denounce Serbs for failing to vote in the plebiscite as being disloyal to the Serbian cause?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not denounce them, but until the end of 1993 some things were such that you could realise that those who did not know, who had not known, whether to take part in public gatherings or not, that those were people whom you could not trust for anything. They could not be trusted when it comes to the plebiscite in Bosnia and Herzegovina or other things. Those people probably took part in all kinds of plebiscites and referendums that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was strange because it was difficult to understand, because someone who would vote for a plebiscite for Yugoslavia could later vote for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that one should know what he really wants, whether you want a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, a Yugoslavia, whether you want to live in Bosnia, in Herzegovina or not. At least, such were the circumstances in which we were at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were not denouncing people for intellectual contradictions; you were denouncing them for failing to vote in the plebiscite because in so doing they were declaring unmistakably which side they were on, is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in a later period it became clear that they were on nobody's side. They were not on the side of the Serbs or Muslims. They were just pursuing their own interests. Those were such people. They were just sitting on the fence and they did not know what they wanted. From time to time, they would side with the most extremist part of the Serbian population and then later they would ally themselves with the most extremist part of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You wrote to President Karadzic and others that Goran Babic had refused to participate in the Serbian plebiscite, but voted (as did his whole family) at the referendum for the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, declaring in unmistakable terms what side he was on. You wrote that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did write something similar, but the information that you have in that report is based on everything that had taken place before -- throughout '92 and '93. That is, on the basis of some reports that were accessible to me at the time, I was writing that report, and those reports were made during the sessions of the Local Commune Assembly in Kozarac, Executive Board of the Local Commune of Kozarac and so on. That is how people declared themselves. The Secretary of the Local Commune -- as the Secretary of the Local Commune, I was in charge of taking minutes of those sessions and meetings, meetings of the Council of the Local Commune, and on the basis of that I composed that document. It is not always -- it does not always represent my personal opinions, but it is also something that testified to what people thought at that time in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told this Court that you made no distinctions between Muslims, Croats, Serbs and others, but in fact you denounced Serbs for various reasons for disloyalty to the Serbian cause and, as part of that denunciation, you made sure that authorities knew whether or not they were married to a Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In your work report did you not denounce Ljuban Lukic and, as part of that denunciation, did you not write to President Karadzic and others that he had been married to a Muslim woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not writing to Radovan Karadzic. I never had an opportunity to exchange any correspondence with him or talk to him and, as far as that information is concerned, it is based on the events that took place in the period between -- in the period when our Local Commune was constituted in Kozarac, exclusively on that basis, and the information that was in the written reports of the proceedings, and Ljuban Lukic, 10 minutes before the death of Ostoja Baltic, was in his company, and it is very likely that in some way he contributed to his murder. He was one of my assistants and he was killed shortly thereafter. What happened, I do not know, but it was discussed at the session of the Local Commune in Kozarac. Maybe because his wife had close relationships with the Suljo Suljic, he was a known criminal, maybe that was the reason why people believed that he was a man who is collaborating with all sides and damaging ordinary people. I know that he was one of the people who wanted the Local Commune of Kozarac to come back and he was -- he, therefore, perished as an innocent man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You wrote this work report. It was copied to the President of the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, among others. You denounced Ljuban Lukic and, as part of that denunciation, you made sure that the main board of the SDS, that the President of the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, and that all the other groups you sent it to, including the chief of the public security station in Banja Luka, knew that he was married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody knew that without that information. I was not disseminating this information. I just said who I sent the whole report and that was in the report of the Local Commune in Kozarac. This is something that I was part -- it was part of my job. I was not deciding what was right or wrong. It does not reflect my own view, what my thoughts, my views were. That is known to the people with whom I talked. But, as a Secretary of the Local Commune, I wrote what was there. I do not know why this person was denounced because he continued to live in Kozarac in a Muslim house. He even -- his house was not even destroyed. He lived in the worst part of Kozarac. Now he moved to the centre of Kozarac and this person continues to live there to date. He was in the police before, he is in the police today. I do not think that I contributed to his denunciation. Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You denounced Brane Koncar and, as part of that denunciation, you also made sure that the information that he was married or had been married to a Muslim woman was included? That is in the report too. When you condemned Goran Babic, you made sure that the people to whom you were sending the report knew that his wife was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was well-known. There was enough information. Everybody knew who was who. Those are -- that is redundant information. Those are the facts that existed. I did not invent that he was married to a Croat. That was known and that was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you wanted to denounce the new policemen in Kozarac who had been, according to you, appointed by Dusan Jankovic, you also made sure that everyone to whom you were writing knew that they were all related to Croats and Muslims; that was part of the denunciation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they abused relationships that they had with Muslims and Croats by not treating them fairly. My brother was married, one to a Muslim, one to a Croat, and that is a fact too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But it is true that when you denounced the new policemen you made sure to put in that they were all married to Muslims and Croats? That is in the report, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it is there, that is probably how it is. That was based on how things were. You could not say that somebody was not a Muslim if they were a Muslim or a Serb if they were not a Serb. That was well-known in Kozarac and elsewhere. That was not a secret. It is a different thing whether people abused their family relations for individual private gain. I was not in such a position. I think that through those family connections they had access to many things that Muslims did not have access to. Maybe at the time I did not understand that, but later I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were in contact with Serbs who had been in Kozarac shortly after the conflict. For example, you met Milan Vlacina in Kozarac on your first visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He had been in Kozarac shortly after the conflict was over. In fact, he had been there so soon after that he was there to see Muslims being taken by buses to Trnopolje and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that, but I do not know whether his story is based on what he saw or what he heard. That, I cannot know, but that is what he told me. On that day when we sat down, we were drinking beer in my cafe and he told me that. I really cannot know whether that was true or not, but that is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to knowing some Serbian soldiers who arrived in Kozarac immediately after the conflict was over, you knew some Serbs who participated in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only man that I saw on that occasion, the others that I met in passing, I did not know them. I do not know if I may have seen one or two other people but Kozarac was empty. It was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you later had an opportunity to talk to Serbs who were soldiers, and some of them told you that they had participated in the conflict in Kozarac or others who were with them told them they participated in the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1993 many things became clear and I found out a lot of information about it, but when I started working in the police reserve they were not talking openly about what had happened. Only later, sometime in early '93, I found out -- we found out a lot of things that we did not -- had not known about before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May this be presented to the witness in reference to one of the confidential Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Show it to the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. (Handed) This is the man who testified in Court as Witness W, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was one of those who told you that he participated in the conflict in Kozarac, in central Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not. I think he never spoke, at least, he never told me. He spoke publicly about some events, but not to having taken part in the conflict. I remember him saying that he was arrested when he went to the village of Vidovici, that he was shot at when he was visiting ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I am not asking for everything Witness W ever said to you, but only whether or not he told you that he participated in the conflict in central Kozarac. You have answered that. As a matter of fact, you learned from ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was in a village. I think he at the time lived at his sister's. Earlier, much earlier, he went to his sister's, to the village. I do not know what the name of the village is. I think Podgradje. That was his sister Dusanka and he was there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you learned from Witness W and others that he was part of a group led by Duca Knezovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war in Kozarac he was on the front as a member of a group under the command of Zoran Karlica. He was on the front in Slavonia somewhere, but not during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That group led by Dusan Knezevic participated in the war in Kozarac when the conflict began. That was something you learned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the early July of '92, when I was on duties in Orlovci, I heard that his brother was killed, that Dusan Knezevic, that his own brother, he was killed -- he and several other people were killed near Kozarusa. So he was a well-known fighter in the Prijedor region. He was in Slavonia on the front and then later there. Those where the stories that were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You learned that the group led by Duca Knezevic participated in the war in Kozarac, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They probably did. I cannot say with certainty. I do not have the real information there, but that was the story. All the people who lived in Orlovci with whom we had contacts and those who worked there before who knew him, they showed him to me sometime early July in 92. He always drove a Mercedes. He did not communicate too much with the people. He would pass and nobody would stop him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That group led by Duca Knezevic also included Zoran Zigic, you learned that as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You learned that this group led by Knezevic often visited Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were stories in the city of Prijedor, there were stories, during 1993. Many things were being told that people had not been telling earlier, and Duca at that time was very powerful at the time and maybe people in order to sort of put him down, they were telling these things. He was a man who was feared in the city of Prijedor. I know that -- at least this was the story -- he and his men at one point broke, smashed, all the cafes in Prijedor. In Prijedor, there was confusion. They did not know who the authority was. Sometimes it was the military police, sometimes it was -- sometimes nobody had the authority. I think that he and his men were, sort of, borderline paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked you some questions or a question or two about Milan Vlacina. He was Nada Vlacina's husband, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Nada Vlacina -- you had a good idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Milan Vlacina was someone you saw in Kozarac on the first day you visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was a tank Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not know, even though he told me. Whether he was a Commander or a member of the crew, I am not sure, but in any event he was part of the crew, the tank crew. When I walked, once I saw him by the tank. That tank was right at the clothing factory and I walked by and he came. But I know from earlier that Vlacina often during '91, there were several attempts to mobilize him and I know he had problems with nerves. He went to therapy in Banja Luka. So he refused to go to the front. That, I know. I know that on one occasion he was even taken to a place near Prijedor. He told me that. They told him, "You are the Commander of this unit", and there were some rocket launchers and that, and he said, "I never knew how to command". He was a very, highly educated man and it was a practice then in Yugoslavia to give highly educated people commanding positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While he was in Kozarac during the conflict, he saw the men of Momcilo Radonovic, "Cigo", transporting the population from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we ought to establish whether the accused is aware of this rather than facts about the person being mentioned by my learned friend being put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The question is, did he see that happening? He can say "yes" or "no", he did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will put the question in another way then, your Honour. That is fine. [To the witness]: You are aware that Milan Vlacina was able to see the men of Momcilo Radonovic (who is also known as "Cigo") transporting the population from Kozarac during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Cigo" (or Momcilo Radonovic) was someone who later became the deputy of the municipality in Prijedor, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early in '93, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You are also aware that, in addition to seeing Muslims being bussed to Prijedor and Trnopolje from Kozarac, Milan Vlacina was also in a position to later see people being bussed, Muslims being bussed, to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what is the truth of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is what Milan Vlacina told you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean on the day when we met in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the day you met in Kozarac or during later conversations, is that not what you learned Milan Vlacina had seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1992 he never told me about these things, not in '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You are aware at this moment as you are testifying to this Court that Milan Vlacina was in a position to see Muslims bussed from Kozarac, not only to Prijedor and Trnopolje, but also to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not so sure that he was in that situation. I had no way to verify whether this was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the mere fact that he told you that makes you uncertain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He told you that though, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1993 he said a lot of things, but during 1992 he did not mention those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: According to what you have told us ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And when I saw him, he was in a state of shock of sorts. I did not see him sitting in a tank. I cannot say. I said what he told me, that he was a crew member of that tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You saw the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but many people bragged, so I cannot guarantee. I was not in a position to see him in the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told this Court that you were at your checkpoint in Orlovci on the Prijedor/Banja Luka road during July?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tieger, before you move into that area of questioning, we will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we recessed, I had asked you about July 1992 when you said you were at the checkpoint in Orlovci on the Banja Luka/Prijedor road. In mid July 1992, you were aware that the last significant pocket of Muslims left in opstina Prijedor were gathered in the area of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, there were nearly 20,000 Muslims gathered there, people who had fled from other parts of the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the first time I hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You are aware that they are not there any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I have never been to Hambarine in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You are aware that the Hambarine area is a wholly devastated area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that it had been shelled, but I don’t know in what kind of a state it is. I think it was on the day when I left Prijedor, on 23rd May, at least such were the stories, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How far is Hambarine from the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. I have never been there. I have heard of Hambarine, but I have never gone there and I could not even tell you what road to take to get to Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have never been to the brdo from Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many hills around the town of Prijedor. I do not know which one you are thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The brdo where the villages of Rizvanovici, Biscani, Hambarine, Carakovo and others are located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard those names but I have never been in those places -- never in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The cleansing of those villages began on about July 20th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not see bus loads of Muslims being taken from the area of Hambarine down the Prijedor/Banja Luka road toward Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Maybe once or twice I saw some buses, but I do not know where they were coming from, from which area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were the people on those buses positioned? Were they sitting upright and looking around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had their heads bent with their hands behind their heads, and they did not stop in Orlovci. They just drove through, but you could notice that, and I know -- I saw that the driver was wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A military uniform of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whose army it was, it was just a military uniform without any insignia. I did not pay attention to that. It was not within our jurisdiction. We had nothing to do with people in uniform who were passing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While you were at the checkpoint did you ever hear the sounds of machine gunfire for any extended period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the sounds of automatic rifle fire for any extended period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the end of July, my colleague, Cvijic, once shot in the air when two vehicles just drove through and did not stop. So he shot, and that was the only shooting incident at the Orlovci checkpoint. Later, I never heard anything similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question was, did you ever hear machine gunfire or automatic rifle fire coming, not necessarily from the immediate checkpoint area, but from anywhere in the area where you could hear those sounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a camping caravan located at that checkpoint so that the traffic policemen or the military policemen could get some rest or some sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I started my duty at Orlovci there was nothing at that moment, but later the military police brought some -- a trailer and they were using it, but they did not use it for sleep. The trailer was used mainly as a kitchen, to eat there -- at least, that is how we used it, me and Cvijic and Brdar. We never had the possibility of sleeping there. I know that the things we had with us we would usually leave them in the car which had taken us to work and, as far as I know, neither the military police slept there. It was not common. I think nobody ever thought of doing such a thing. At that time in June/July, well, most of the time we spent outside. We did not even sit in the car. It was difficult to stay in the open. We were afraid. So, on one side of the car there was a small shelter and we mainly spent time there and we would move it, we would never be at the same place, and we would stay awake all the night in case of night duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During your earlier testimony, you discussed at some length your involvement with the group of Kozarac citizens which met on two occasions with the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. Is it not true that you met, not just on those two occasions with the Crisis Staff in Prijedor, but there was a third occasion when you met with the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not true. Only two times we met. Aside from that, I do not know whether you are referring to the civic forum. If you are referring to the civic forum, we met twice. As for the citizens of the Kozarac Local Commune, we had another meeting at the beginning of August when we filed a request to revoke the decision whereby resettlement of Kozarac was prohibited. It was with Bosko Mandic, with the President of the Crisis Staff, but that was not the same group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am referring to the civic forum. Is it not true that before the meeting between the members of the civic forum, the people from Kozarac and the members of the Krizni Stab, the Crisis Staff, you met privately with the Crisis Staff Commander, Stakic, and with SDS President, Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not true that I met with them privately. It was a meeting -- it was the agreement we had reached during the first meeting. It was an agreement with the residents, with the members of the civic forum. We once talked over the telephone with them. It was Susic's telephone. Then we waited again and then we called again. They did not want to receive us. They said that if we are talking about the same people, we would not receive anyone. So I talked to Susic. I wanted to know who would be present because I had never attended meetings of the civic forum before, and he told me approximately who would be in the group. He said that the people who had negotiated before would not be there, not the same people. They told me, "You should go there" and then I said, "OK, I will go there one hour earlier and then you will wait for me, and I will go out and then later on I will tell you whether we will be received", because there was a possibility of not being received at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were the one who contacted Miskovic and Stakic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they told me to do so, and that is what we did. It was part of our agreement because when I first talked to them over the telephone nobody wanted to talk to me. They did not connect me to anyone. The man on the switchboard, he said, "What kind of agreements are you talking about? Those talks are over". So when I went there I told them about the delegation of the forum. I told them who the persons were, some positive things about them. I also told them that those were not the same people who had negotiated before, but later on it turned out that there was one person there, Ilijaz Memic, who had had talks before. That is what we realised at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1992 you had a police uniform, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I started to work at Orlovci, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What other kinds of uniforms or uniform did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the same uniform, as I described previously, the summer uniform in the form of overalls. That is what my brother had given me before in Banja Luka. When Kusota, Kusota, when he deserted, gave me the rifle, he brought some bag with parts of the uniform that he had, which means -- the uniform was the SMB uniform but that I never really wore it. I left it in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you had a police uniform, the camouflage uniform you described, and an SMB uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have the SMB uniform. I left it in Kozarac and I never took it. I never went to get it because, first of all, it was not my size. This man is smaller than me. I would have maybe taken it if it had been the right size.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your attorney asked you a question about the interviews which were conducted both after your arrest in Germany and then here in The Hague. The German authorities were also interested in the question of uniforms. They advised you that there were allegations that persons who participated in the conflict in Kozarac had worn camouflage uniforms. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible. I do not recall exactly, but before the conflict in Kozarac I saw many people wearing uniforms, camouflage uniforms, but it is a general term. I do not know what they were referring to, whether they were referring to blue camouflage uniforms, green ones or yellow ones. It is a general term, "camouflage uniform", for all kinds of uniforms that could be used as camouflage uniforms. So it was not very clear what colour they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The term "camouflage uniform" does cover a range of possible colours, as you have indicated. But the German authorities asked you, "Mr. Tadic, do you own a camouflage uniform or other military uniform or have you ever worn one?" You told them, "No", isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You described the ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can my learned friend actually recite the full answer that the defendant gave in answer to this question, as it does not just end at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be pleased to. As a matter of fact, Mr. Tadic, what you told the German authorities was this. They asked you, "Mr. Tadic, do you own a camouflage uniform or other military uniform or have you ever worn one?" You said, "No, no, as far as the camouflage uniform goes. As to the rest, some qualifications are called for. During my activity in Orlovci, during the day time I wore blue trousers and short sleeved light blue shirt also with police insignia, and at night I also wore a jacket. Now, this is the uniform of the police unit I was serving with. Owing to the insignia and the uniform I was wearing, an outsider would in no way conclude I was in the military but would categorise me as a police officer".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I told.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you wore a camouflage uniform, at least you have admitted wearing a camouflage uniform, at the checkpoint itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What they were referring to, I do not know, but at that time I thought that they were referring to a military uniform, a multi-coloured uniform with stripes, green stripes and blue in colour. I do not know what colours they were. I was not referring to a spotted type of uniform and I did not think that that was a camouflage uniform, because it is a type of camouflage uniform that you wear on top of regular uniform. Personally, I do not know that uniform, who it belonged to, the one that I was given by my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When were you given that uniform by your brother, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was before I went to Trnopolje. I first talked to him and then he gave me this uniform and then I went home. I put it on. Then I left with Jovo and left. It was after the incident he had had in Kozarac, we were told that we should not move around without uniform after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Tadic, the three uniforms you refer to, the police uniform, the spotted camouflage uniform, which you say your brother gave you and the SMB uniform that you say you received from Kusota, were not the only uniforms you had, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a uniform, a police uniform, a winter uniform, which I did not use most of the time. It is a very thick type of uniform. It is a blue one that we were issued in Prijedor, but we did not wear it at that time. Sometimes at night, yes, but it is all part of police uniform and I do not remember having any other uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You received in that bundle from Kusota, according to you, not only an SMB uniform but a camouflage uniform, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it was there. I never used his uniform. I said that I had received that, but it remained in the house and I never used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You made reference in testimony to an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is the rifle you took with you to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you get that rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it before from Kusota. He is the owner, Mile Kusota, and it was given to me by his brother Rade in Kozarac. I think it took place at the end of '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is what your wife has also told us and your brother has also told us, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your wife and your brother also told the Court, testified to the Court, that you got this rifle from Kusota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, because my wife should have known that because she received from Kusota's mother some beans because they thought that that would relieve his son of the military duty in Croatia. That is why she should have known about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 148, please? This document is a certificate whereby it is certified that Dusko Tadic, rank soldier, has signed out an automatic rifle, with the number given, with 300 bullets, and that that weapon and ammunition were issued to you for the purpose of carrying out the given orders. It is signed and stamped by Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic on behalf of the Territorial Defence for the municipality of Banja Luka on May 4th 1992. This document was found in your house after your arrest when German authorities searched your house, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you get this paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got this paper from my brother Ljubomir in Banja Luka on the date which is indicated here. I filled it out myself in Banja Luka. This information here, Tadic Dusko and other data, were handwritten by me. He had given me a blank, an empty form because he knew that I had a rifle in Kozarac, and people were saying that those weapons would be taken away by the authorities in Prijedor. So he was afraid that it might happen, because it was not only a question of having your weapons taken away; there was also a problem of mobilization, or I could have been also punished somehow because I did not have any papers for that weapon that Kusota had given me. So that is why my brother gave me this form and filled it out and I took it to Kozarac. So that is why I kept it. As for the quantity of ammunition, it is just a rough quantity. I do not know whether I really had the exact amount of ammunition. I know that Kusota had given me two cartridges, but I just put here 300, just like that. I did not think too much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Kusota gave you two cartridges, as your wife testified, but you wrote down 300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I got this form from my brother in Banja Luka. It was empty. It just had a stamp and the signature here. It happened on the day I evacuated my family. It was on 3rd May and I got this paper the next day, the 4th May '92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if you can find out what a "cartridge" is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Tadic, by "cartridge" you are referring to the clip that goes into an automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Each clip contains how many bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many exactly, I never counted them, and I do not know. I never had the opportunity to shoot out a clip so I did not really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have heard other testimony in Court that there are 30 bullets in a clip. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think there are that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify something you talked about at the end of your direct testimony. When you left Prijedor, you went to Banja Luka, in 1993, when you finally left Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in August?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long were you in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time. I stayed throughout September and I think I left for Belgrade in October. At that time again there were several reasons. First of all, you could not leave easily because the controls were very strict, so my brother again found a certificate for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, sorry to interrupt you, but I want to stick to one question at a time. How long were you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think until the beginning of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you go from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay in Belgrade I visited the Red Cross, the UNHCR seat and the Human Rights Committee of the United Nations in Belgrade. Only after that did I leave Belgrade. I mean, I left Belgrade for Nuremberg. It could have been around 20th November. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did you get from Belgrade to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By coach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long were you in Nuremberg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed overnight in Nuremberg and the next day I spent it in Nuremberg as well, and then I left to Munich with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I want to discuss with you the period of time around the time you were mobilized or around the time you indicated in direct testimony that you were mobilized. You testified that on June 15th, a Monday, you left Banja Luka early in the morning by train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were traveling alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I travelled alone. If I stated otherwise somewhere, I probably made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were met by Vokic in front of the police building. After a discussion with Jankovic and Prpos, you were accepted into the reserve force and then you spent that night in Prijedor at Vokic's place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Friday, I told them that I would come the next working day and I talked to Vokic and then he met me, took me to Dusan Jankovic for an interview. It was all in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of June 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That night you were at Vokic's place and that was the only night you ever spent at Vokic's place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later I was coming to his place. I do not think I slept there, but I was coming to his place where he lived with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next day, the 16th, you were on duty at Orlovci on the Prijedor/Banja Luka road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you also testified that you fetched your wife and brought her to Prijedor on 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that that is that exact date, but anyway, I knew that she had to report to work by June 20th. I know that once after the duty, went to Banja Luka and I brought her back. There was a truck that was going towards Serbia, but I am not sure if that was that exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you testified that was on your second day of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly. It took place before June 20th. That, I do know, because that was the deadline for her to report to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you went to Banja Luka to get her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She did not dare come, knowing, based on her previous experience. There was a curfew in Prijedor at the time, 10 o'clock till 5.00 in the morning. There was no movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you spent the night in Banja Luka with her and brought her back in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then when I visited her? I am not sure about the date really. Yes, yes, the first time. I went there twice to get my wife during June of 1992, and once she came by herself with her -- with my mother and the children and they never went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, it was your recollection during your direct testimony that you went to fetch her from Banja Luka on the second day of your duty, 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that it was the second day of my duty. At first, I was not sure whether my first day on duty was Monday or Tuesday, what was counted. I was not sure whether I was mobilized on a Monday or Tuesday. Then later in the book I saw that it was a Tuesday, so I cannot be sure whether I went there on Wednesday or Thursday. I cannot say that with any certainty. It is very hard to remember that date. It was not anything significant. There was nothing significant. I know that after that I went to duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the day you fetched your wife from Banja Luka and were on duty at the checkpoint, that night you and your wife spent the night at the home of Martin and Mileva Dzaja, correct? You have testified to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came back we slept together in the house of Mileva Dzaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your wife told us that she went back to Banja Luka the next day, the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it was the 18th. All this took place, her coming and her return, all took place before June 20th, but I am not sure if it was on 17th, 18th or 19th, I am not sure. It is true that she returned to Banja Luka by herself, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let us look at what you said about those dates before, Mr. Tadic. You have referred before to interviews which were conducted here in The Hague.
