Those interviews were conducted by Mr. Reid in the detention facility at Scheveningen. You were warned, advised of your rights to remain silent before the interview, each interview began. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I asked to talk, even before in Germany and here also. That is no secret. I wanted to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your lawyer was with you at all times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I asked for those interviews. I asked to testify here. I do not think I have anything to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You spoke about coming to Prijedor from Banja Luka to Mr. Reid. For the benefit of counsel I am referring to page 58 of the December 22nd interview. You told him that on 15th June you were staying in Banja Luka together with your family. "On that day, as also before, we lived in a house in the street of Koste Jarica. On 15th June 1992 I was in contact, that is I spoke with my wife, Mira Vidovic, that is Mira Tadic, with Ljubomir Tadic, with Slavica Tadic, with Zlatko Bajic." You also talk about a number of other persons you talked to, about being in the restaurant Skala. That is in Banja Luka, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those days I had contacts with those persons, but I do not know if it was all on the 15th or the 14th or some other date. Anyway, those were the persons with whom I was in contact in Banja Luka at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you continued to describe the events of that period of time to Mr. Reid on that occasion and on other interviews. In May, on May 10th in fact, you discussed your mobilization. Now I am referring to page 76 of the May interview. You told him: "I remember that on June 16th in the morning I came with my brother to the centre of Prijedor." That is your brother Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought of him, yes, I had him in mind. I know that I travelled with him from Banja Luka, but then on that first day, I cannot remember the exact date, but on the first day of my mobilization he was not with me. He only went to Kozarac twice and then was coming later to Prijedor, but he was not there on the date when I was mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "I came with my brother to the centre of Prijedor. Radovan Vokic, a policeman, took me to the Commander, Dusan Jankovic, and staff Sormaz. Then I was told, they told me that I would be mobilized in the reserve unit of the traffic police. I had then met the Commander of the traffic police, Djuro Prpos. I handed over my illegal rifle that on the same day was issued to me by the police. Signed out. He told me that I was free then and that I should report to work tomorrow morning. I know that I had spent that night at the place, at the apartment, of Radovan Vokic and Dusanka Vokic." That is what you told Mr. Reid in May. Now you also discussed the same period of time in December with him. On that occasion in December 1995 you said this, did you not, Mr. Tadic. Page 74 of the December interview. "On 16th June 1992 I came with my brother Ljubomir by train from Banja Luka, and I was mobilized by traffic, reserve traffic police in Prijedor. After I was formally mobilized, together with my brother and Radovan Vokic, I went to the town centre and we went to a cafe bar next to Hotel Balkan where we had a drink. Afterwards I noticed in the street Beslagic and after sometime I called or I guess I invited my brother together with Meho Beslagic. We went to the cafe restaurant Aero Club where we sat in front of the Aero Club in the terrace at Aero Club where we discussed the previous events that took place in Prijedor and in Kozarac. Now sometime before 1 o'clock p.m. my brother Ljubomir took the train and left for Banja Luka. I stayed for a short time with Meho Beslagic and we also agreed to meet again in the following days. Now between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m. I was in the apartment of Jelena Gajic and Zare. I had lunch there. I also speak with Milka Gajic. Now also on that occasion it was the first time that I had seen Nevenka Tadic and Jasminka Salkanovic and her son, the first time since the conflict broke out. Also present was Zare Gajic and his aunt, Dzaja Mileva. Now somewhere between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. I went to the apartment of Radovan Vokic and there together with his wife, Dusanka Vokic, we had dinner. Then we stayed for sometime up and then went to bed." All on 16th June, the day you say you were mobilized in these interviews, the day you said you were mobilized in May 1995 and December of 1995. In fact you have said on a number of occasions, have you not, that you were not on duty the first day you were mobilized, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not on duty when I came to Prijedor and that was something that was not fully clear to me. I was not sure about the date. I thought that that was the date that I was mobilized. But I was mobilized on the day when I started my duty. The quotes, what you quoted, there were such meetings but maybe not on the dates. What I have described, it is difficult to know whether it was on 16th or on another day. But in June I met Meho and I was in the Gajic apartment and I saw those people and my brother was coming and we sat together with Meho, but it not all of this could have taken place in a single day. I told what happened and with whom I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let us talk about what happened then on 17th, or at least what you say happened on 17th or said happened on 17th when you were interviewed in May and December. Page 51. Here in another interview you talked about being mobilized -- for the benefit of the interpreters it is sections 113 through 115. They have some markings and they can follow more easily. You described again in detail -- I am sorry, this is December -- again in detail what happened on the 16th, and talked about how you and Ljubomir went to the cafe bar restaurant, Aero Club. How Ljubomir left back to Banja Luka, you went to the Gajic family apartment and then spent the night of the 16th and of the 17th, those nights you spent in the house of Radovan Vokic and Dusanka Vokic. You said how, "I can remember very well that on 17th June 1992 in the morning I, together with Radovan Vokic in an official car we left. We went to the police station in Prijedor." That is what you said in December '95, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. I thought that it was 17th and it is always about the first day when I came to Prijedor, and when I went with Vokic to -- and that date was also entered as the first date of my duty in my military book. I simply said what I thought. I thought that that was that date. I could not remember the right date, but the event is correct. I first went to duty with Vokic from his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well then, let us talk about June 18th. That is the day your wife told us she went back to Banja Luka after the two of you spent the night at the home of Martin and Mileva Dzaja. On page 59 (reference numbers 119 and 120 for the interpreters), you described again the 17th in great deal. As to the 17th June 1992 you say: "I would just like to say one more thing which I remember very well, and that is after my, after I finished my duty controlling the traffic post in Orlovci, I went to Pecani, to the settlement of Pecani, planning to sleep, spend the night in the house of my friends, and in the settlement of Pecani I met with Nada Vlacina and that was somewhere between 4.00 and 6.00 p.m. and her husband Milan Vlacina. I remember he was not at home. He was on duty because he was a reservist in the army. Then from there I went to the apartment of the Gajic family and then decided to spend the night at the apartment of the Vokic family." That is your description of 17th. You go on: "As to 18th June 1992, I can tell you the following. I was a member of the reserve police in Prijedor, was a member of the traffic police in Prijedor. During the day I mainly stayed in the town of Prijedor and on that occasion I had contacts with Jelena Gajic, Zare Gajic, Mileva Gajic and with Salkanovic Jasminka and her son and with Nevenka Tadic. From in front of the police station in Prijedor I went on duty together with Miroslav Cvijic and Miroslav Brdar. We went with the police Golf which was driven by Miroslav Brdar and I was on duty from 9.00 p.m. till 7.00 a.m. the following morning."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The descriptions are fairly correct, but not the date. I really do not know the date. It is hard, it is hard to remember the date. I had contact with all the people in the way that I described, but I cannot recall whether if it happened on that date. But it happened during June 1992. I would eat lunch every day with Jelena Gajic and any time I was free, and that is where I would meet people that I quoted, and I know that when I visited Nada her husband was not there and so I had planned to spend the night there, but then I decided otherwise. So those were the people with whom I met there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us see what you said about June 20th. Page 16, reference 121. "As to 20th June 1992, I went to my duty post in Orlovci together with Miroslav Cvijic and Miroslav Brdar. I was on duty as a reserve policeman, traffic policeman, controlling the traffic on the road from Prijedor to Banja Luka from 3.00 p.m. till 9.00 p.m. Apart from those persons with whom I had mentioned previously on that day, and also on the following days, during my duty hours I had contact with Slavica Aleksic who would every day go to Prijedor where she worked as a waitress in Hotel Balkan, and also after finishing her work in Prijedor she would go back." You mentioned Djurdevic Mirko. "I would go from Prijedor to another location where he worked and then back again." You mentioned Milomir Stakic, the Commander of the Krizni Stab who worked in Prijedor but lived in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were the people who were passing through the checkpoint every day. There is a mistake. Mrs. Lukic, I did not know her last name at the time well, but Mr. Reid insisted on the dates and so I tried to remember the dates the best I could. I am not sure that they were right, but the events I described are all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Reid insist that you tell him on more than one occasion, "I remember very well"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he did not insist that much, but I tried to make it -- I knew that if my lawyers co-operated with the authorities of Republika Srpska, I knew that there would be documents, that there would be exact dates of my duties and one day if this co-operation came to be that it would all be made public. I tried to remember. I could not remember all the days. I tried to create a picture of what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You had those documents during your interview with Mr. Reid, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, again, I would again sign them all and I would again tell the story. The events are true. The dates I could not remember. That is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to move on to -- let me just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what documents were you referring to when you said that Mr. Tadic had them during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By "those documents", Mr. Tadic, I am referring to the rosters that were introduced into court. Those are the documents you had during the December interviews, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if I had them. I do not remember. Maybe I did have them. Maybe I had them. I tried to remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be moving on to a new subject. It will consume more than five minutes, I believe, so I can partially cover it or ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions now about the time period between May 23rd, the day before the attack on Kozarac, and the date you say you were mobilized. You testified before this Court that on May 23rd you travelled with Trivo Reljic and others to Prijedor and from there took a train to Banja Luka at about noon, and once in Banja Luka you went to the house on Koste Jarica Street. You indicated that you returned to Kozarac during the period of time before you were mobilized, and you said on page No. 5967 that you returned to Kozarac on June 1st by train with your brother, and then returned that same day to Banja Luka at dusk after being at Lamovita and in Kozarac. You also spoke with Mr. Reid about this time period as well -- you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall. We discussed everything, but I do not know specifically what I did not -- I was not paying attention. There were several questions relating to 1990, '91, '92, so it is quite possible that we discussed that period as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also possible that when you talked to Mr. Reid about the first time you say you returned to Kozarac after leaving on May 23rd that you said you went back at the beginning of the first week of June and stayed at the Timarac' house for several days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would it be helpful if I read the specific references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is OK. I believe you. It is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Reid a second time about the time period between May 23rd and the date on which you say you were mobilized, did you tell Mr. Reid that you returned on May 30th, went back to Banja Luka the same day, stayed one day in Banja Luka and then returned to Babici again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible again. When it comes to dates, I cannot say anything. I know that the first visit to Timarci, Lamovita and Kozarac took place before I went to Trnopolje. Trnopolje is the period which I can recall with most certainty. I know it was a weekend and I know that this first visit took place before that. I know that because in that period I met in Banja Luka, in Starcevica neighbourhood, I met with Kahrimanovic and I talked to him and he told me that should I go there once again that I should visit his house also. I remember that I said to people in Trnopolje that I had been to Kozarac. When I met to Turkanovic and Ferid Gunjic, they asked me about Kozarac and I told them I had been there once and I described them what I had seen. That is how I remember that I visited Kozarac only once before I went to Trnopolje. I cannot tell you exactly whether it was on the 1st. It is quite possible, but I would not be surprised if it was otherwise. I could not remember dates. That is why I keep referring to that visit to Trnopolje, because there were several mobilizations in that time, and the mobilization which took place on 16th was rather important and I know that it was a weekend when I went to Prijedor when I was mobilized into the police, and I believe that there had been an attack during the weekend at Prijedor. I know they were discussing the state, the war state, in Prijedor and I remember I visited the family house of Gajic family and they showed me some holes in the walls and they were saying that there had been an attack on Prijedor. That is why I remember those events, but I cannot tell you the exact dates. It is very difficult. It is difficult even for those who mentioned dates here in the Court. It is difficult to tell with certainty. The same is with holidays, you tend to remember certain holidays, the 1st May or 25th May, which used to be Tito's birthday. Those were the dates we would often remember, remember easily. But, as for any other dates, it was quite difficult unless you had some official documents like military books, the official documents which can be found in the Prijedor town hall. If I had those documents, I would be more specific, but I cannot simply forget my meeting certain people and what we discussed and so on. I told you about the places I visited and the people I spoke to, but it is difficult to say -- for example, when it comes Hambarine, I can tell you with certainty that I have never been there. That is what I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us forget specific dates for a moment then. The German authorities were also very interested in this period of time, the period of time between shortly before the attack and the date on which you say you returned from Banja Luka to Prijedor. They explained to you that they were interested in it because there were allegations that you had been in Kozarac and participated in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not talked about in relation to the conflict. I was only accused for alleged killings of people in Omarska. There were no charges in relation to Kozarac. At that time there was only one alleged act which then was extended and the same pace continued here. At first, Kozarac was not mentioned at all. It was just a general story about the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am going to refer your counsel to page 11 of the second day of the German interviews on which you were asked the following question, Mr. Tadic: "Mr. Tadic yesterday when providing information about the individual, you said that on 23 May 1992 and until 16 or 18 July you had been at your family's in Banja Luka". You later corrected July to June when you saw your military book or learned the date in your military book. The quote goes on: "What do you respond to statements by witnesses that in the meantime you returned to Kozarac and played an active part in the taking of the town by the Serbs?" That was the question. You said: "As far as I can remember, the war began on 24 May 1992 in Kozarac and I did not return to Kozarac in the above mentioned time period".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that answer, although I think that when they asked me that they phrased their question as to -- they wanted to know where I lived at that time, not where I was. We discussed it later on, because it was difficult to explain what their intention was, what they wanted, and the question that I gave them. I realised they were interested in knowing where I was living at that time with my family, and I remember that they claimed that I had gone back to live in Kozarac with my family. So when I was relating about those events, I was referring to the life of my family in Banja Luka. We were not discussing -- it is possible that they asked me about an active participation in those events. So I probably gave them a similar answer because I know I had not taken any active part in the conflict in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, perhaps it will surprise you to learn that the Germans anticipated this problem and assertion and so pressed on and again asked you,: "I am now asking you again expressly, in the period in question were you only in Banja Luka and nowhere else?" Answer: "I was only in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, their question was, "Did you live in Banja Luka and nowhere else?" and my answer was always, "I lived in Banja Luka", and not "I was". I was in Trnopolje and they put the same question in relation to Trnopolje, and they asked me in a similar way about Trnopolje and Orlovci, but that is different. I thought that I lived in Banja Luka until the moment my family moved to Prijedor. I did not have anything in Prijedor. I did not have any clothing and I was living at various different -- at various places. That is what I had in mind when I answered. It may have been interpreted in a different way, but that is what I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, you told the German authorities that you slept in Banja Luka every night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in Banja Luka I slept in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could not be that I was either in barracks or at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you spoke in your testimony at page 4992 of the transcript that you wanted to report yourself as a refugee in Banja Luka, but you could not because there were some laws of which you were not aware. Indeed, you tried to but they told you there was no way, that first you would have to report to a military office. In fact, on an earlier occasion you attempted to explain the fact that you were not on the refugee list in Banja Luka in a different way. You said on a previous occasion that the reason that you were not on the refugee list was not because you tried to register, but because you were ashamed to be a refugee, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, both are correct, but in any case I tried. I remember taking some food from the Red Cross at one occasion and together with my brother I brought that food to Starcevica. I was ashamed of having done that, let alone being on their list. I was not considered to be such a poor man which I was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When asked about that by Mr. Reid, you only told him that you were ashamed to be a refugee, not that you had tried in any way to get yourself on the list? It is only here in Court that you have tried to say that you made an effort to do so, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is possible, but I did not insist to be put on that list. I asked, I enquired, about the procedure because my family could not obtain the status of refugees through regular procedure because they told me that, "We do not have anyone from Prijedor, you are the only ones". So it was simply not possible. All the rights that I could have, they told me that I should have them in Banja Luka. When I left Prijedor, I cancelled my residence from Prijedor and you have in my identity card "residence cancelled", I believe it was in July, in favour of Banja Luka, but I could never register in Banja Luka, and when I asked they told me it was not possible. I needed certificates from the military office. The priority was the military book. It was a law. You could not do anything without a military book. If you wanted to have any rights whatsoever, it was impossible without that. So each time, and I said I had proof that my family house had been destroyed in Kozarac, and they told me that I should go to Prijedor and have my rights regulated there. So I would go back to Prijedor to get some kind of status and it was simply impossible, and I realised that it was impossible to obtain any rights if you were not a member of the army. When you asked me about the people of Muslim nationality, the same procedure, the same law, applied to everyone. The law of Republika Srpska did not specifically state. There was a general law that only those people who had taken part in war had the right to obtain status. So a wife, for example, could not obtain a job if she did not have a certificate whereby it was certified that her husband had been a member of the army. It was a general procedure in Republika Srpska at that time and I think that the same situation was elsewhere, and that very procedure forced people to leave. That is why I had to leave and I think that many Muslims and Croats had to leave the area because of that, not because they were being evicted, but simply they could not regulate the rights of their status if they were not members of either the military or the police. At that time companies were not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you discussed the procedure by which you obtained accommodation in Pecani. You described how you went to the town hall, asked for accommodation, said you were with the police, which was a kind of condition, and the clerk sent you to Pecani to the commission in charge of making lists of apartments available. Did you receive any kind of special treatment to get this apartment of Hasan Tulundzic or did you just go through the normal procedure that a reserve traffic police officer would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not only a procedure whether you were military or policeman. You simply had to be somewhere to be a conscript, either a member of the reserve force. It applied to anyone, to members of Crisis Staff and so on. If you wanted to leave or travel to Prijedor or Banja Luka, you just needed a certificate, you needed something. First, you had to present, to produce, the military book. At that time it was considered as an identification card. My treatment was the same as the treatment of any other people. Only those who were members of the police or the military could obtain the same rights. That was some sort of unofficial rule, and when I discussed that with the person who was in charge, he went to talk to someone and when he came back he told me that he had met with the President of the Executive Council and later on, when I said after a certain period when I moved there, I told them that I did not have a written decision to be there, and Miskovic said, "Well, that is not a problem, nobody has a decision". When I went there, I did not know whether the apartment used to belong to Tulundzic or someone else. I simply had no other place to take my family to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I asked you earlier whether or not -- in fact, the question was, "The group led by Dusan Knezevic also included Zoran Zigic, you learned that as well?" and you said, "No, I did not know that". Referring now to page 18 of the December interview, this was another matter you spoke to Mr. Reid about in December 1995. You told him -- for the benefit of the interpreters, your Honour, reference 101 -- "Now, according to what I have heard, Zoran Zigic participated in the war in Croatia and later on when the conflict began in Prijedor, he participated in ... that, when the conflict began in the area of Prijedor, that he participated in the war in Kozarac and that he was together in a group with Dusan Knezevic". Those were your words, is that correct, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I said that. At the end of 1994 I was interviewed in Germany as a witness in the case of Zoran Zigic, and they asked me about him and I told them what I knew in relation to that man. So everything I said I repeated there, and this is what I heard before I left the Prijedor municipality. As for some specific proof that they really were in the same group, I do not know, but those two people were notorious in Prijedor, especially after the murder of certain civilians in Prijedor town, after what Zoran Zigic was arrested and convicted in Banja Luka. I am not sure whether he was rally convicted or not, but that is what I read in the papers in Germany. Those people are well-known in Prijedor. I did not have any contacts with them. I am just telling you what I heard. Whether it is correct or not, I do not know. I did not know who Zigic was and I do not remember whether I ever met him. As for Duca Knezevic, I used to see him in passing either in town. He was driving a motorcycle. He never walked on foot and I never saw him as a civilian. The first time I talked to him, it was in October '92 when he came to Kozarac, to the Local Commune, together with his father and his uncle. They were asking about some plums. I do not know. They were asking for a service at the level of the Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I also talked to you about Milan Vlacina earlier in the day and asked you about what he told you and what you were aware he saw about seeing people transported from Prijedor. You said, "During 1992, he never told me those things, not in 1992". You also said, "During 1993 he said a lot of things, but during 1992 he did not mention those events". I refer your attorney to ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- page 20 of the December interview at 103. You talked about Radonovic Momcilo, same person known as Cigo. You say: "Radonovic Momcilo is the same person as this Cigo. What I can say about him is that the first time I met him was in the autumn of 1992 in Prijedor. Previously, I had heard about him from my colleagues at the duty post in Orlovci, and what I heard about him was that he had participated in the war in Croatia and that he was also the leader of a military unit whose members were mainly men from Orlovci. "Now, in connection with the events that took place in the Prijedor municipality, when I met Milan Vlacina in Kozarac he told me that he had seen Radovan, Radonovic Momcilo, actually that he had seen the men of Radonovic Momcilo transporting population from Kozarac". Then you added that you were not a member of Radonovic's military unit, and that you had met him while he was a deputy in the municipality. Those were your words too, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is quite possible that this is so, but I did not say -- I did not mention Orlovci. I think it was Omarska. I do not know whether I said that he was the leader of the group from Orlovci. That man always lived in Omarska, not in Orlovci. It is possible that I made a mistake. As for the description that was given to me by Milan Vlacina, that is what he told me. Whether he told me that on that day, I do not know, but he told me that he was in Kozarac when that happened, but I cannot claim here that he said that on that particular day. I did not consider it to be an important piece of information. I do not know whether he said that in December or in January. I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I also asked you earlier about any occasions on which you saw buses transporting prisoners on the Prijedor/Banja Luka road. You said maybe once or twice you saw such buses, and described how the prisoners were positioned in the bus. You said they just drove through, but you could notice that and "I know I saw that the driver was wearing a military uniform". Next question: "Was it a military uniform of the army of Republika Srpska?" You said, "I do not know whose army it was. It was just a military uniform without significance. I did not pay attention to that". Referring your counsel to page 62 of December 22nd 1995 interview conducted by Mr. Reid with Mr. Tadic -- these are references 122 through 124 -- he also asked you if at any time while you were on duty you saw buses, and you said the following: "Only once I believe that I noticed a bus only with men, and also I noticed that on the bus were men from the security of the army of Republika Srpska, men in uniform". Those were also your words, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I think about it more closely, that is what I think I said. I cannot say with certainty, but the driver, if I can recall, the driver had a beard, as far as I can recall, but I cannot -- I cannot say if that is so. But if -- that he had a uniform, yes, I saw a driver. I think that there was also some security there, but it was just a glance. I did not pay much attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Security of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An assumption, who else could it have been? The question is strange. It could not have been security of the Bosnian Army. What else I should have said? I know that they were not policemen. That is absolutely correct. They would not have been in a blue uniform. What else could it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As long as we are on the subject of uniforms, we also discussed that earlier. You referred to the three uniforms that you had, the police uniform, the spotted camouflage uniform (which you say your brother gave you) and the SMB uniform you received from Kusota which you said ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not own an SMB uniform. That was the uniform that stayed in Kozarac. I do not know what period you are referring to. I did not drag that uniform together with children's clothing. It had no significance for me. I was not a conscript to take my military equipment with me, and that rifle I had was exclusively in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I asked you whether or not you received a camouflage uniform in addition to the SMB uniform from Kusota and you said "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you had only received an SMB uniform from Kusota along with a rifle, no camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is how it was, and the uniform that I got from my brother I did not consider it a camouflage uniform. I did not consider it anything. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me refer you and your attorney to page 47 of the May 10th interview with you and Mr. Reid. Reference is 26 through 28. You describe the weapon and how you came into possession of it from Kusota. Then you say that, "He came back carrying on his back a big bundle which was wrapped in linen". The investigator asked, "Sorry, a big bundle of what, weapons?" You said the following: "No, no. Later I saw that actually inside was a rifle, uniform, boots, the regular army, the regular equipment that is issued to a soldier, and also I remember that there was a classic uniform and that there were also boots, and there was also a uniform of mixed colours, yellow colours". So that was another uniform which you had in your possession in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. I am not sure. I cannot say. I only looked at that equipment and then left it. Even the boots that I got were not my size.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You agree that you told Mr. Reid that you received a camouflage uniform in addition to an SMB uniform when Kusota brought the bundle that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not get the uniform that Mr. Reid thinks about, and I think that that is what Mr. Reid thinks about. The yellow thing I did not get from him. That I can say with certainty. Maybe I did not -- I did even say so, but it is not important whether I got a yellow SMB or something else. I know that the uniform that he brought I never used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I would like to satisfy you that the words were not Mr. Reid's but were yours and, in fact, were not suggested by Mr. Reid who was simply asking you a question about what you received. So perhaps you would like to look at your exact words? May I have this marked for identification and shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need for that. I believe you. What I am telling is what I know for certain. Maybe I have said that way, but I know that it was not so. I do not think that there was any significance. When Mr. Reid and I talked I was not accused of anything regarding uniforms. Even if I had 10 uniforms, maybe I would have said there was something like that. It was insignificant. I am not accused of having a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: My recollection may be in error, but I thought the witness in evidence in chief said that in the bag there was the SMB and there may have been a camouflage uniform. Did he not say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I checked the transcript, your Honour. I will be happy to read that exact portion as I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, as a matter of fact, you had enough uniforms that you were giving them away. Do you remember giving one to Mirko Vidovic in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I started working with the police, it was not a big problem for uniforms, the one that I described. There were some reserve uniforms, auxiliary uniforms, and I gave one to my wife's brother. I was not in a position to give them out to others. Whoever was in the reserve police had an opportunity to get a uniform. As far as that uniform is concerned, I said, as far as I recall, at the time when we talked, I did not consider it significant whether it was in a bag or somewhere else. I thought that it was insignificant as a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You yourself wore a camouflage uniform at the checkpoint, in addition to your blue police uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That uniform I wore exclusively when my uniform of the reserve policemen was being laundered. I did not have two summer uniforms for the reserve police. I got it from Vokic Radovan. I do not know the date, but I got it from him and the winter one I got at the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Referring your counsel to page 83 of the May 10th interview -- for the benefit of the interpreters, I am looking for the reference number, just below 85 -- on that occasion you were asked to describe the uniforms you wore at the checkpoint. You said the following: "As far as I remember, during June of 1992, I mostly, mainly, wore a multi-coloured yellow uniform. The top part and the down part was the same colour." Those were your words, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I recall, sometimes I wore that kind of uniform too. In any respect, I had police insignia on all of them, regardless of whether it was a yellow or a blue one. On each of those uniforms on the shoulder there was an insignia. There was "police" insignia written. I really cannot say how many times in June I wore that uniform and another one, but those are the reasons. There were no other reasons why. That was the only reason why the laundering of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is why you wore mainly in June your yellow camouflage uniform. Let me ask you some questions about ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that that was the reason. That was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the one that Mr. Tadic said had an insignia on it, is that the one that his brother gave him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, did you hear the Court's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that question. When I started working in the police in Prijedor, we all got insignia, the police insignia, especially the word insignia, that are very conspicuous. It is about 10 centimetres wide, half circled, blue background and white stitching in Cyrillic letters "Police". We also signed out to the blue berets with the insignia, a metal badge of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, how many times were you in Trnopolje camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to remember. I think I was there five times. I do not mean the camp -- you talked about the "camp". I do not know what you mean under the "camp", but in Trnopolje I was about five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where in Trnopolje were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was with Jovo Samardzija, as I said earlier, over the weekend in June of '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Please ask me specifically. I do not know what you mean under a "camp", so I am not in a position to answer. Is it the whole complex or was it the street that I was passing on? It is not clear to me what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you inside or at the site of Trnopolje camp with Mr. Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please say specifically? If you show me photographs, there were some photographs seen here, and if you show me the photographs, I will show where it was. It is not a secret. Some people are saying that the camp was the school building, some say that it was the entire complex. So now I am not sure what they think when they say the "Trnopolje camp". So, please, if you can be very specific with your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you visited with Mr. Samardzija, were you on the grounds of what had once been the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never -- neither at that time nor later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you on the street which runs immediately in front of the school within the boundaries of where the former school was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the summer of '92?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At any time in '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in the summer. I said I was there five times. In the summer of '92, I was exclusively only once with Jovo Samardzija and I know where I was and whom I met. I know that I saw then -- I saw people who I grew up with and that is what stayed in my memory. Hiba Hankic, my neighbour, and her husband, Salih, I greeted them; greeted with Gunjic Ferid and I talked to him -- he still lives in Prijedor today -- with Osman, Sahib Kulasic. They all asked me what happened. I did not know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were those people free to leave the area they were in, the area of Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if they could leave. We did not talk about that and again I say I did not meet them at that space where you say. I met them in the street, and some I met in front of the ambulance in Trnopolje, the space in front of the ambulance, ambulanta. In 1992, I was never in the school yard of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you told investigators on previous occasions, either the German investigators or the Tribunal investigators, that Trnopolje was an open area and people were free to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time when I visited with Jovo Samardzija, that was my impression. What happened later, I do not know. Whether the status change in the summer of '92, I did not go there. When I saw -- neither my neighbours told me that it was very difficult for them, neither did I get that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please tell us the other four occasions when you were in Trnopolje and, please, you can tell us what part of Trnopolje you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that once I was there officially. I do not know, again I cannot say the exact date, but it was the moment when the refugees from Trnopolje were going to Karlovac in organisation of the Red Cross, the UNHCR. That was the first time that I went there on official business as a reserve policeman. I stood by a bus and my job was to help in -- to the Red Cross in its activities. I know that there was a young woman who was reading names off a list. She was in front of the school building. People were passing by her one by one and were getting on the bus. I know that we -- I remember that we stayed almost all day. It was raining and I had a blue cape and Goran Babic, the Commander of the police station in Kozarac, was with us and about 10 other policemen who had similar duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about the other three occasions you were in Trnopolje, when were they and where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all in the period between the fall, that is, the end of 1992. On one occasion I remember I went to Trnopolje. First, in Prijedor I met Adil Jakupovic's wife. We often visited more often, more often than this gentleman stated here. Every other day or at least once a week we visited each other in Prijedor. On one occasion when I went to his wife, to their house, she told me she was not at the old address any more. So I found her at another house that was closer, and she said that Adil went to Trnopolje with one of the sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was that? When did you visit Trnopolje on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was the end of October 1992. I cannot say with certainty, but I also know that it rained again and the weather was pretty bad. We stood by a house up the road, up the street, and we talked. I know that Zonjic -- he is also a reserve policeman. He is a refugee from Bosanska Bojna. He was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When were you in Trnopolje on the remaining two occasions you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly the date. On one occasion I was there with my brother. At that time I worked as a Secretary of the Local Commune and he came to Prijedor with Hamdija, his friend. They came from Banja Luka. That Hamdija had a friend in Kozarac, and he said, "Oh, let me come along". He wanted to find a friend of his. I think his name was Rega. I had heard of him. He was a salesman. So we went together to Trnopolje. He talked to some people and finally found out that this man had been in Slovenia for quite some time. That was one time. Also, I went as a Secretary of the Local Commune with Popovic Joso. I asked him to give me a ride to Trnopolje, because before that in Prijedor I got many messages from the Red Cross. I went to the International Red Cross and they gave me about 20 messages of refugees. Somebody from abroad were writing to people who were the natives of Kozarac, and the representative of the Red Cross gave me those messages and he said, "All these are for people from Kozarac, so there". I left that with the policeman on duty whom I found there and we returned, Joso Popovic and I. I think the policeman's name was Petkovic. He was in the part where the restaurant used to be, across the street from the ambulanta, the health clinic. I do not know if I ever went there again after that. I remember seeing Adil Jakupovic on later occasions in Prijedor, and he said that he never managed to go there, that he got registered with the International Red Cross. It was his intention because otherwise he could not leave Prijedor in a normal, regular manner. The only way would be something unofficial, through the military or if you get a letter of guarantee from abroad, the other members of the family would write to the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, just focusing on Trnopolje, what were you wearing on the occasions you were in Trnopolje other than the time you described being there as a reserve policeman or the time you visited with Mr. Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. Sometimes I -- I remember when I went there on official business I had a raincoat of blue colour. When I went with Adil Jakupovic, I do not remember what kind of uniform I had. On other occasions, I went in civilian clothes, normal clothes that you wear. It was the fall and so I know that it was warmer clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the occasion when I was doing -- I was on security detail for the International Red Cross, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have indicated you have some trouble remembering the dates. You just know it was sometime between the fall and then you did not specify what time period. Do you know whether or not you were in Trnopolje in October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that around October 1st those refugees left for Karlovac. My birthday is on October 1st, but I am not sure that it was on that very day. I think there were maybe -- or maybe it was 31st, maybe it was 2nd, maybe it was 1st. I am not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not you were in Trnopolje in November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible. As I said, I do not recall exactly because there were very brief visits, except for the time when I was there officially. Then that day I was there from morning till dusk. The representatives of the Red Cross handed out food to the refugees, but they could not give us any. We could not give food to the police and the military of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not you were in Trnopolje in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I am not sure. I know that I think I was there about five times altogether down there, but it was not the -- I never entered, though, the space, as you claim. The closest encounter with people there was in the street with people that I knew. As far as I know, people moved around freely in the street. I do not know what rules were there at the time. When I was there with Adil Jakupovic, I know that people moved about freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you in Trnopolje in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, from the fall, that is, during the fall, I was there about four times and once during the summer. I know my reasons. I know why I went there. I know with whom I had contact there. I cannot say exactly when I went there the first time. In fact, I know that when I was there on official business it was when part of the refugees were leaving. I think it was 37 or 38 buses that were leaving Trnopolje. As far as the other visits, were all to the town of Trnopolje. Maybe they had other rules there, but I was exclusively in the street and I know with whom I talked and why I talked and I never went there alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, with respect to the uniforms you wore when you were in Trnopolje camp, Mr. Tadic, did you not tell the German authorities that on four occasions when you were in Trnopolje camp you were uniformed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I said that. I did not think it was important. I know why I went there and I know exactly with whom I went and I know with whom I met there. I know that I was there once officially and that was then. I cannot tell you the exact date with certainty, but I know that I was there on that occasion when those people were leaving Trnopolje for Karlovac. I know there was a white van which was parked there. It was an UNHCR van. I talked to a representative on that occasion and it was a Frenchman, and I also know that there was a representative of the Red Cross there. There was the Red Cross there who visited me in my detention unit. He told me that, indeed, there was a French representative of the Red Cross there at that time. I would have never gone there officially had I not known that there was an International Red Cross office there and that the UNHCR was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier we discussed the rifle and the certificate which was placed in front of you which indicates the certification for issuance of a rifle and ammunition. You stated that you received this paper from your brother Ljubo in Banja Luka on the date indicated there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I requested a similar certificate in Prijedor. I used to know a man by the name of Slobodan Bokan and I asked him for a such a paper, and he did give me a certificate of some sort, but the certificate that I have seen here, it is the certificate that I was given by my brother in Banja Luka. I tried several times to obtain a similar certificate in Prijedor because I saw that many of my neighbours in Kozarac had similar certificates, and Fikret Tulundzic showed the same certificate to me, except there was not the "Territorial Defence, Banja Luka", but the "Territorial Defence, Prijedor", marked on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us talk about that for a moment. In fact, you were asked about that in an interview with Mr. Reid to be found at page 48. It is reference Nos. 30 and 31. That should be May 10th interview. "Can you explain the following about that certificate, Mr. Tadic?" "Yes, that automatic rifle stayed in my possession and that same rifle was signed out when I was assigned to the reserve traffic police. Now, as far as this automatic rifle is in question, in April '92 I spoke to Simo Miskovic and I told him about the rifle and asked him what I should do with it and he told me that I should keep it until the police comes asking for it. But at, by the end of April, the local residents of Kozarac had been saying, or whether they were just rumours, that all weapons, unauthorised weapons, to be found in the houses will be seized, confiscated. So, on one occasion when I went to Prijedor, I do not know exactly when, I spoke to Bokan Slobodan who was a reserve military personnel and I told him about it and then he gave me a certificate, just like that, an empty certificate, that I had been issued a weapon. And since I was not mobilized, the origin of the weapon could have caused problems, so somewhere, around the beginning of May, I filled out that certificate in my own handwriting and I put down my own name, so that it would serve me as a sort of guarantee regarding the origin of the weapon". First of all, those are your words, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it happened, but it is not the same certificate I have been talking about. I was given a certificate from him. I forgot. I did talk to Miskovic, but I cannot tell you it was the beginning of '91. I think it happened at the end of '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is not the certificate that you were examining which is Exhibit 148?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is a similar certificate but the title was different. It read "Territorial Defence, Prijedor". The other one is "Territorial Defence, Banja Luka".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So at the beginning of May you filled out two or you actually forged two similar certificates for this weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not forge it. I do not know why you think that I forged it. The data on the certificate are OK. The number of the rifle was important, nothing else. There was a kind of guarantee certificate of the origin. The fact that my name was there -- well, I see no other way I could have done that. I did the same thing as many of my neighbours did, nothing special. None of us never hid weapons, neither did my neighbours hide their weapons from me. Later on they were openly carrying weapons. They talked to me about everything. I had no secrets with my real neighbours. The only thing is that I could not contact with people who had had a criminal record from before and who were dangerous for anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, apparently, then you were aware of Serbian civilians being armed by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why do you think it is clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. There were all kinds of stories. I cannot deny that. There were stories that people, both from the SDA, SDS, the green berets, were being armed. There were all kinds of stories. Which of them were true, I do not know. It was obvious that people were armed and that they were obtaining weapons, whether individually or in some other way, that is a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us pursue this just a bit more, if we may? So in May 1995 you told Mr. Reid about the certificate you say you got from Slobodan Bokan, but you did not mention the certificate you received from your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody asked me about that. I had other certificates that my brother had given to me. I had a certificate to travel to Serbia, for Belgrade. It was a similar certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In Court you mentioned the certificate you received from your brother, but not the certificate you received from Slobodan Bokan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had someone asked me, I would have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That certificate was found in your house when the German authorities searched it after your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember what was there, but when I fled Prijedor I just took everything I could. I put them in a bag and left. The same thing happened when I was leaving Banja Luka. I did not know what to take until the very moment I was leaving for Serbia. If my departure had been normal, I would have probably not taken. I did not think it was something dangerous. Those are the facts. I did not say that I did not have a rifle, that I did not have a certificate. It was the certificate that was filled out with me and I am not responsible for that. If you think it is a forgery, then it is a forgery, but I was never really a soldier. It is true that a soldier is mentioned there, but I have never been a soldier. If you think that I was a soldier, well, please, you can check on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tadic, I only meant it was a forgery in the sense that you are saying you filled it out rather than an official filling it out. In any event, the Germans seized that document and they interviewed you. They asked you specifically about that document, a document which said you were a soldier, which said that you had been issued an automatic rifle, which said that you had been issued 300 bullets, which said it had been issued from the Territorial Defence of Banja Luka, and they said: "Mr. Tadic, what about that document?" You said: "I do not know anything about it", isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is true, according to the description you just gave, but that is the way they described it. But my answer is, no, it is true I was not given the certificate by the Territorial Defence and I was not given the weapons by the Territorial Defence. I was not a soldier of the Territorial Defence. That is not true. What is true is that I filled out that certificate and I was not asked about that. It is true that I was given a blank form and all other details, other all data, that I was a soldier member of the Territorial Defence, that is not true. On the basis of that paper, I do not know. I do not know how you reached the conclusion that I was a soldier of the Territorial Defence because of that paper. Such data should be found in the military book. Ever since I served my military duty, regular duty, in the JNA, I have not changed my military book and all the relevant information is there in my military book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The German authorities asked you about the certificate referring to an exhibit number and they asked you: "What about that document?" You said: "I do not know anything about it", isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what happened. The description that they gave, I do not know anything about that. I did not receive the weapon from the Territorial Defence, and that was my answer. How they described it, I do not know anything about that. That is correct and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, that interview was interpreted for you throughout the entire process of the interview, was it not, and after each question and answer you and your attorney were permitted to object to it or to add to it, if you wished and you signed off on that page, your signature appears on that page, isn't that all true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is true what you are saying, the fact that I had the right to add anything I wanted to, and I asked for something to be added. You can ask Mr. Sklebitz. I wanted his assistance to add something, something that I thought that had not been adequately described. I am not saying that the certificate was not discussed, but it was not presented in the same light as I presented it here. The German authorities, when at the end of '93 we talked about the case, they wanted me to give a statement in the case of Zoran Zigic and I said, "I will accept if you allow me to add what I think should be added to my previous interviews". They said, "OK" and then we sat down and they even asked a Minister of some kind to come there and he gave his approval. But that policeman told me that we would first discuss the case of Zoran Zigic and then we would later discuss what I wanted to be discussed or to add. I agreed and then we discussed the Zoran Zigic case. After that when it was -- when we had to discuss our previous interviews, when I wanted to add something, when I heard -- when he heard what I said, he said, "No, it is out of the question. You said everything you had to say". So I was not given the opportunity to say during that interview, I do not know anything about interpretation, but there are quite a few things that are not correct. The very title "Local Commune Territorial Defence", I do not think that German authorities knew about things, that they knew what was what. Their objective was just to question me for ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You speak some German, do you not, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so. I do speak some English now. I have learned it in my cell, although I do not have much communication with the outer world, but I can understand some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not speak to the guards at the detention facility in Germany in German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did communicate with one of the guards sometimes, but before, before my departure, when I knew that I would be transferred here. Nobody talked to me before that. They would just tell me, "Go back to your room. Do this or that". They just communicated in that way. I sometimes asked them for help, but it was not a correct attitude towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: However much German you speak, you certainly do speak enough, would you not agree, to know the meaning of "Ich weiss nicht"? That is not too complicated? You can say and understand "I do not know" in German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand you. I did have an interpreter when I talked to the German authorities -- that is beyond doubt -- but I just said -- I just described the way they talked to me, the way they behaved towards me. I know that Mr. Reid said if there is anything I want to add that I would have the opportunity to talk later on, and that is what I was told in Germany. But they did not allow me later on to discuss anything. I am not saying it is -- I do not claim that what I would say later on would be completely true. I was just trying to tell what I could remember. I am not saying here that I did not make any mistakes. I do not think anyone can remember all the dates. I was accused several times and ever since summer '92, and they kept asking me, "Where were you on the 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th?" and so on, in the morning and in the evening. I was not a robot and there is nothing I can say in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked you earlier about Witness W and whether ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you go on to Witness W, maybe 10 minutes ago you made reference to a certificate that the German authorities asked about, then much else was discussed. It is still not clear to me what certificate they were talking about. You referred to an Exhibit number and then there was a long discussion about something else. Maybe I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I will try to clarify that, your Honour. Thank you. Just to clarify, the document the German authorities were referring to when they asked you about the certificate issuing you a rifle and 300 bullets is the same document that was seized from your home in Munich and the same document that we have looked at here in Court today, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that document in Munich during the interview. I was described that document in a different way. There are certain things that are written there and that were described in their own way, but the reality was different. Whether they were thinking of this certificate or some other certificate, I do not know. That is why I said that I do not know what they were referring to. That is the way they described it; that I was issued the rifle by the Territorial Defence, for example, that I was a soldier of the Territorial Defence. Those were their questions. They did not show me the certificate and that is why I gave them the answers that I gave them. This is the first time I am hearing this story, the story that you told here. I have never seen that certificate, the way they described it, and I do not know which certificate they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just so it is clear, sir, the interview with the German authorities which you signed which was contemporaneously interpreted states: "Exhibit 1.12.87", your Honour, which is the German number, "contains a certificate dated 4th May 1992 that Dusko Tadic had been provided by the 'staff of the Territorial Defence' with an automatic rifle AP and 300 rounds of ammunition. Mr. Tadic, what can you tell us about that certification?" That was the question, sir. That was the question to which you answered you knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know anything about it. I do not know whether I was issued with that rifle by the Territorial Defence staff and that was my answer. I was not issued that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I asked you earlier about Witness W and asked you whether or not he was one of those who told you that he participated in the conflict in central Kozarac. You responded that he did not. I would like to direct your counsel's attention to the December interviews, December 22nd, on page 24 -- I am sorry, I apologise, page 69. That should be in the May series, on May 10th. Mr. Tadic, you were talking at that time on May 10th about the conflict in opstina Prijedor and in Kozarac. You suggested that if the interviewer wanted you to, you could give the names of the persons you had spoken to and who had participated in the conflict that took place in the centre of Kozarac. The first name you mentioned was that of Witness W?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I mentioned that name, but it is just an assumption, only because I knew from earlier that that witness had been in the war in Slavonia, in Zoran Karlica's Unit, and it was common knowledge in Prijedor that Zoran Karlica was Commander of the attack on Kozarac. That is why I thought that he might be one of the participants in the conflict. I did not know for sure whether he really was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What you said to Mr. Reid was, "If you want me to, I could give you the names of the persons who had spoken to me and who had participated in the conflict that took place in the centre of Kozarac". Those were your words, not Mr. Reid's, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. It was not a secret. People were talking about the events in Kozarac, but I could not know what was true of all those stories. That was just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you have spoken in evidence about -- I think I am quoting -- "we simple, ordinary people". The fact is that you were not only a member of the SDS, and not a member in name only, but you were an earnest member of the SDS who before the conflict tried to obtain weapons for Serbs, organise assignments for the conflict, obtain information about weapons which the Muslim police might have and discourage Serbs from co-operating with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were people in Kozarac, SDS members, who were not passive members, correct? There were activists, SDS activists, in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew only about my wife and Miso Radulovic. I do not know that there were other members of the SDS during my stay in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Miso Radulovic was the man whom you described as an SDS activist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an assumption. I think it is something that followed from the fact that he was a member -- I think so -- of the board for the plebiscite, nothing else. I am not sure whether he was, but I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Kozarac, Miso Radulovic tried to organise the assignments for Serbs to be implemented should war break out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He talked about the need to evacuate the population, because he used to be a Commander of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, so he knew about the ways to evacuate population. So in relation to that, it was in relation to that that he talked about the needs and so on, that in case of conflict the population should leave in an organised way, because it was clear to us at that time, me and my family, we were not involved, we were not on the lists for shelters. So everything that followed from my contacts with Miso Radulovic and some other people in Kozarac was in relation to the safety of my family and my personal safety. I tried to create conditions to save me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You worked side by side with Miso Radulovic who was an SDS activist to organise the assignments to be implemented if the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not work with him about that. Those were just simple conversations. I do not know in what way I was involved, as you say. I do not think he was involved. Those were just discussions, what if this should happen, if that should happen. But nobody had any solutions in that situation. There was a discussion about how to evacuate oneself and one's family. I participated in those discussions because I did not own a car and I knew that I was not on the list of shelters, so I had to talk to someone. Those were just conversations about what to do in this or that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in the report, however, which you prepared and submitted, in the work report which you prepared for the purpose of submitting to SDS officials and other authorities, you described the following: "Under such circumstances, Milos Radulovic and I tried to join forces and organise the assignments to be implemented which, as arranged, were to come into effect should fighting start. The majority of people with the village of Vidovici as a sole exception refused to co-operate siding with the stronger". Those are the words you wrote to, among others, the President of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina to describe what you did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the words that I wrote on the basis of my work as the Secretary of the Local Commune and the reports that had been drafted for the Local Commune in Kozarac in the period of '92, '93. So all that information is based on the declarations and statements of some people who attended those meetings and sessions of the Assembly or the Executive Board. As for those activities, it is normal that I was concerned about how to save me and my family from that area because nobody knew what would happen. So when it comes to co-operation, I talked to Slobodan Savanovic because he had a lorry. I simply needed to have someone if I wanted to leave Kozarac. So I had to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, before the conflict in Kozarac there were sentry posts and checkpoints which were manned by both Serbs and Muslims, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what period you have -- you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1992, before May 24, when the attack on Kozarac occurred, there were joint checkpoints or joint sentry points in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty that they were joint. I had no particular insight into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you not denounce Serbs who served on checkpoints with Muslims in your letter to the President of the SDS and to others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That letter was composed in 1993 and I do not know in what way that was possible to do. I think in '93, I think 8th August '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You wrote the report on 8th August 1993 and the report encompassed your work for the SDS between the period of time 1990 through 1993, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, but it is based on information that was in the reports created during the sessions of the Local Communes, presided by Jasikovic Branka, at the -- Bosko Dragicevic presided over the Local Commune and in December of 1992 while I was the President, and so it was based on the statements of the members. Those are -- that is information that is not, that is not verifiable. I was not a policeman to be able to verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this report is all about you, is it not? The report begins: "I was born on October 1st 1955 in Kozarac", and it ends with your name, "Dusko Tadic", many pages later? It is about what you did in 1990 through 1993 and it is about your views about what happened during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some parts there are elements, my views, but they are all based on my activities in Kozarac, as the Secretary of the Local Commune. I think that the latter part of that report, it states, "The Secretary of the Local Commune". So, as a Secretary, I had access to all the minutes of all meetings of the Assembly of the Local Commune. This was done pretty fast. I was not a typist. There are many mistakes and one -- maybe that was one of the reasons why I was arrested on August 9th when the authorities in Prijedor got a hold of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wherever you got the information about this person from or these people, you write to the SDS authorities that Mirko Grahovac and his son Zeljko were also patrolling at the checkpoint near the Orthodox church and you denounced them for that, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how I could denounce in August of '93, a year later in the area of the Local Commune of Kozarac, but that information are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Brane Koncar was a Serb who patrolled with Muslims at the checkpoint near the old sawmill and you denounce him for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you refer to Grahovac, that is only a segment. He stole five or six thousand litres of gasoline while, apparently, he was on duty. I do not know how to take those duties if they were not honest, so this person could have looted all Kozarac. I visited his house. I know what his property was like before the war and what it was after. He had three times more. He had livestock and all of a sudden he had 30 cows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Even before you wrote this letter and even before the outbreak of the conflict, you and Miso Radulovic worked together to discourage Serbs from participating in these joint patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were, perhaps, ideas of Miso, but Miso himself gave his hunting rifle to his colleagues who were manning those checkpoints. It is something that was spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were trying to persuade Serbs not to participate in the joint checkpoints and joint sentry points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After our meeting with the municipal Crisis Staff in Prijedor, we, all of us who were there representing the civic forum, we agreed in every contact with the population, we worked hard on improving the trust in Kozarac. So, regardless of whether somebody was a Muslim, a Serb, if you contacted with friends or acquaintances, we told them how to approach them. We said not to wear a uniform. I still stand by it. I met Emir Susic and I told him, "I will give you my hunting rifle. You should not, and I will -- I do not want you to lose your head".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Despite your effort and Miso Radulovic's efforts, Serbs, nevertheless, continued to participate with Muslims in the joint patrols, Serbs like Koncar and Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
