utterances.text: I do not know if they -- maybe sometimes they, they were seen there, because also Miso's son was on the front line from the first day. I cannot say anything about that. If I talked to Miso about it and Miso himself was present at the Assembly of the Local Commune, and he was talking very strictly to all of us who had these initiatives about Kozarac. He was the Commander of the Territorial Defence of Kozarac. He was a native. He was almost 60 years and I assumed that he had experience. Nobody was under age there, so that I would -- should give them advice. Until the last day, I was socialising with my neighbours, the ones that I trusted and who trusted me. Four days before the conflict, I had a barbecue party with Fikret Tulundzic. We had carp and we barbecued carp, and we looked and we thought that everything would pass. We did not believe that things would happen. I knew that he had weapons; he knew that I had them. He sometimes gave me the bullets for my .765 handgun. That was all open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You tried to get other weapons as well; a few months before the war you worked with Vaso Radunjic on trying to get weapons which belonged formerly to the shoe factory and which were stored in the Prijedor barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that event, but I did not take a direct, active part in it. My brother Mladen told me about it, who -- he was in Kozarac four or five months in late '91 and I think my brother was there. He had a van, a Nissan, of red colour. They tried something and nothing came of it. Radunjic was to be fired, he was suspended, and he and his wife who was a Muslim, after the SDA came into power, six months later, he fled abroad. That is only something that I heard. I cannot be sure if that even happened. My brother Mladen could say more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us read the words from the letter which you wrote when you sat down to describe your work for the SDS between 1990 and 1993. That is on page 4. "A few months before the war, I worked with Vaso Radunjic, the secretary in resignation in the shoe factory, on trying to get weapons which were the company's property but were stored at the Prijedor barracks. We had delivery documents drafted and an agreement to be allocated those weapons stored at the barracks, but when my brother tried to load them on to the van Captain Javoric in person accompanied by his security officer, Iso, prevented him. It never went any further from that, though news about our attempt leaked down to Kozarac. "I was able to understand the whole thing only when I found out that the security officer mentioned above was a Muslim from Montenegro, and that it was his ethnicity that made our effort futile, though I was never able to understand why Javoric was allowed then and later to work against Serbs, distributing weapons to Muslims and justifying his work by saying that the weapons were common property".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the description is very clear, that Mr. Radunjic, whether he tried or not, I cannot be sure, but on that day I was there. I know that the brother came back to Kozarac and he told about it. Since I have heard of it, about it, I thought that in some ways I was a participant of it. But, as far as Javoric is concerned, I cannot say much. I heard about him before and after the war and there were also stories that he was distributing weapons to everybody, but not to help, but in order to create an even worse situation, only worse. By the very fact that a tank was at the entrance of Kozarac, it was clear that the tank would be used in the conflict in Kozarac. I think it is absurd to think about fighting tanks with rifles. I do not know who could have thought about that. It is already on May 3rd that the Serbs gave clear indications that they would use tanks in Kozarac. I do not know why, how, what an idea it would be had it not been for the conflict. I thought that it would be best if I left Kozarac, and I think that many left before me following the same kind of thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During 1992 you repeatedly attempted to obtain information on the number of weapons that the Kozarac reserve police had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot say -- you could not say that I tried, that there was -- there were always discussions to return the weapons or not. During our meetings in Prijedor it was discussed. There was always arguments, whether they were secret weapons brought in from Sarajevo or whether they were supplying in another way. But none of this information was verified. So, that information seeped into my head as it did into everybody else's. There were a lot of unknowns. My curiosity, if it existed, it was all based on fear for my own personal security. I knew what was to happen. If I had known what was going on, I would have left Kozarac much earlier. Why did I come back, and I would not have taken my family out if I had any other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, it is not me who says that you repeatedly attempted to do so. I am just reading from your letter at this point, Mr. Tadic, and I am quoting it on page 4: "When I repeatedly attempted to obtain from him information about the number and nature of weapons the Kozarac reserve police had" -- that is what you wrote in 1993 when you prepared your report about your activities from 1990 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was curious, that is true, but that is where it stayed. Just as many were curious about whether I had weapons or whether I knew somebody maybe, what was going to happen, but I did not know anything. That was the exchange of views. I do not think that it was anything very significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you did not engage in these efforts because you were curious or because you were a simple, ordinary person. You did those things because you were an earnest SDS member and a self-proclaimed activist. You describe yourself as an activist in this letter, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could say after August 15 1992 I was, sort of, an activist but nothing before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did these things because you were an enthusiastic supporter of the idea of creating Republika Srpska, and that is what you said in this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every lay person in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there are three constituent people in Bosnia, Croats, Muslims and Serbs had the equal rights and one of the reasons for my being in -- I lived in a place which was 95 per cent Muslim and I never questioned that. Up until 1992, all my contacts were with my neighbours and in Prijedor I never met with people with whom I had not been meeting before that. All people with whom I was meeting know my views. Had I not been thinking well about people in Prijedor and had I not been thinking well -- meant well for people in Kozarac, I never would have become active in a way I did. Sometimes maybe people joined sentries in order to show to their neighbours how they felt, but I was never in those sentries myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you outlined all these activities to the officials and others whom you intended to receive this letter and you told them how you had worked since 1990 in order to contribute to the creation of a common Serbian country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this letter -- it was created in August, 8th August, 1993, and I had been arrested at least 10 times by the authorities that you describe. At the entrance of the city hall in Prijedor, I was again arrested and after that I had to leave Republika Srpska. That is a reflection of my understanding after that letter, that I still had -- that it was still a big tragedy. I had no task. That letter, it was written in a very simple way and it is all based on the Assembly of the Local Commune proceedings. The continuity between 1993, you can see there, there is '93 and then there is 1990. That letter was not directed to the authorities of Republika Srpska. They were only -- I also visited the United Nations office in Belgrade and I talked about that and nobody was really interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After those efforts (some of which you detailed in the letter), when the time came, May 24th, that the Srpski opstina Prijedor would be cleansed of Muslims, you continued to contribute as an activist in places like Omarska, Keraterm and Jaskici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only the contribution to the revival of the Local Commune of Kozarac and, as far as the ethnic cleansing is concerned that you talk about, I do not know what my departure and what the departure of my family from Republika Srpska means, if that is not ethnic cleansing. I did not leave there, because I had it good there because I had some merits, because I thought I left because I did not think that I could really rely on people. I know very well where I was moving. I may be wrong about the dates, that is true. I may be wrong about some descriptions, whether a sleeve was blue or whether the uniform was blue or yellow, but I know where I was all my life. I cannot forget that, and I cannot be wrong whether I was in some location where I had never been in my life. I can be wrong about the date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the cook, the carpenter, the florist, the home maker, the businessman, the school teacher and dozens and dozens and dozens of others from Kozarac, from Kevljani, from Prijedor, from Hrnici, from Jaskici, from Sivci, they are all wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you have in your mind. I do not think that anybody is guilty. Many who came here suffered, but I did too. There is no difference there because I was a Serb and they were Muslims or Croats. All the people who suffered are those who did not want to fight in the Serb Republic on the front line. Those activities were not deemed to anything much in the beginning, those political activities. People who were -- during the communist period everything was taken over from the old system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I am talking about the dozens and dozens and dozens of people who saw you in those locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe they saw me in Prijedor. Many of my neighbours whom I saw and with whom I visited, they could see me there. They could see me in Orlovci where I was doing my job. Some of them I even met in Banja Luka, it is true. They could see me on TV images when Monika Gras made her film, and she edited the footage of '91 and puts it in as if it was '92 and then repeats it every week. It was, it was there repeated in Germany every week. My winter uniform and the summer in Trnopolje, that is what she has cut together. So that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Tieger, would you go back regarding the certificate that the German authorities showed to Mr. Tadic. You have mentioned a particular Exhibit number and I still want to make it clear in my own mind what certificate we are talking about and whether or not that was shown to Mr. Tadic by the German authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I read to Mr. Tadic from the text of the interview and that is as far as the testimony went. If the Court has a question about the relationship between the Exhibit number referred to in the German interview ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will just ask.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, the certificate that you have discussed and Mr. Tieger asked you about, and the certificate I am referring to is the one that indicates that you have been issued an automatic rifle and 300 bullets. You have testified that you received that from your brother Ljubomir and that you actually filled in your name and the amounts, etc. When you were interviewed by the German authorities, was that certificate shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not shown to me. They described it to me and phrased the question in a way whether I had received it from the Territorial Defence in Banja Luka, "Did you get it as a member of the Territorial Defence Unit?" And I said, "I hear about such certificate for the first time". It was about signing on a weapon. So that is -- and not what my brother gave me which I filled out and which Mr. Prosecutor calls a forgery.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you had not received it from the Territorial Defence, that is what you are saying? You had received it from your brother as you have testified today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the blank certificate and I filled -- I got it from my brother and I knew the number of the rifle and it matches the serial number of the rifle that Kusota signed out on. I think that that can be verified.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have additional questions in the light of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, nothing arising from that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked a series of questions about the interviews with the Prosecutor in May and December 1995 and those were interviews conducted by Mr. Robert Reid. You were asked, or it was put to you, that you had documents there at the time of the interviews. Just so it is clear to us, we have had documents in this Court, but I would like to ask you this: were the lists and the official duty plan that we had produced with the names of people at checkpoint Orlovci as well as the list of names in the schedule with you during that series of interviews in May and December 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have that document. The one that Mr. Wladimiroff provided, that was given to the Defence. I think that Simo Drljaca was the chief. I had no reason to believe him and so I did not regard that document at all. I was talking about what I tried to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have before you during the December or May interview a letter that had been provided by Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, exactly when that took place, there were two pieces of paper with Simo Drljaca's signature and Mr. Wladimiroff put in front of me, and I said that I could use it if I wanted to. I told him that I did not need it and that was sitting next to me. The official documents that I saw, the official working lists, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, the documents that we have had produced in Court showing those on duty at checkpoint Orlovci in the official duty plan as well as the schedule of names with the times and dates were not documents before you during those interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you now to look at the work report. If 344A could be provided in your own language before you. 344B, if the Bench have it, is the English translation of that document. Before it goes before you, perhaps if it could be handed to me so that I can find the appropriate passage? If you could look at the text at the top of the page that I am putting before you which is at the foot of page 7 of the English translation? Perhaps if page 7 of the English translation could be put on the overhead monitor? If it could be moved up the screen so we can see the foot of the page? When I raise my hand, if you could turn over to the next page? Mr. Tadic, if you could read out from the top of the that page? I believe it starts: "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992". Do you see that at the top? Could you read that what is written in the text there in this work report or letter to Dr. Karadzic? Can you read it out, please, in your own language to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992. One day before that" ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992, and one day before that I had left for Banja Luka where my family lived as refugees in an abandoned house living off of our last saved food. I never took part in the attack on Kozarac because, despite everything after I had been living among those people for 35 years, I still did not see why I would have to shoot at my former neighbours when, surely, things would change with time because the truth will come out and because I did not see that all had to end in destruction and devastation. Mere luck saved those few Serbs who had not been organised and the unexpected chaos in the green berets. I came back to the Kozarac in June of '90 and immediately joined the reserve police force in Prijedor on the traffic police patrol at the checkpoint in Orlovci".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does that mean the translation is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. I am re-examining him on a document that was put before him in relation to his activities at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, but there are two lines that appear in the English that were omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am just going back to that, your Honour, as I was able to notice that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. KAY (To the witness): Could you read it more slowly? I want you to go back to the position of "living among those people for 35 years" which I think you will find is about the fourth line. Just read it slowly, not at 100 miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I never took part in attack on Kozarac because despite everything, after I had been living among those people for 35 years, I did not see why I would have to shoot at my former neighbours, and in time the truth will come out whether it all had to end up in destruction and devastation, this setting up and looting of people's property, disregarding of who the previous owner was. Mere luck saved those few Serbs who had luck".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just stop there. Can you just go back a sentence and please read it slowly so that the translator can catch your words. Go back to the "35 years" and just read it slowly. Just start at the "35 years".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I never took part in the attack on Kozarac because despite everything, after I had been living among those people for 35 years, I thought that I should not shoot at my former neighbours, and that in time the truth will come out whether it all had to end in the destruction and devastation, in setting up camps and looting of property, disregarding of who the previous owner was."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, that is all I ask in re-examination. Great reference has been made in the cross-examination to the two interviews that took place in May and December 1995. I would ask that those be made as Exhibits before the Court in the form of the English translation, so that the Court is able to see the full extent of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have heard a lot of statements and they have been used throughout the trial. I suppose in cross-examination we never received all of the statements though. What is the position of the Prosecutor? Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It had been our intention to tender that document in the course of our rebuttal case, but if the Court wishes it now we do not have any objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will wait until the rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I anticipated that was the case as I know Mr. Reid is being called at the rebuttal stage. It just occurred to me it would be useful for the Court to have it now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It might be better to come in in the orderly way so we can receive the benefit that whoever is going to offer it wishes us to have. Is there anything else? Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We do not have any witnesses for today, but it looks as though we will get through our business at a fairly early point tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I understand from Mr. Bos. Mr. Tieger, you are standing still, do you want to contribute something or did you have additional questions? I do forget, I am sorry. We got on to other matters about the Exhibit. Do you have any recross, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, with respect to the letter that your counsel referred to when asking you about the rosters and dates, that letter was a timetable of the times and dates at the Orlovci checkpoint, is that correct, the timetable of shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that it was a list -- you do not recall the letter at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember two pieces. When I saw the signature of Simo Drljaca I left it with my family. I was not interested in that, because I was not sure whether his information was accurate. In view of some previous events I believe that something may be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you not have that document with you during the December 22nd 1995 interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you allow me, if you show me that, I could tell you. It is not a letter. It is just two pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be marked for identification as Prosecution next in order? Mr. Tadic, this is the timetable of shifts, among the timetables of shifts which accompanied the letter, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen this paper, but I do not know which letter you are referring to. It is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this is among the documents you had with you on December 22nd 1995 and which you referred to during the course of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point Mr. Wladimiroff did give me such a sheet of paper with this information, so I had it with me. Yes, this is the document. I just do not think that the signature was the same. I think it was -- yes, timetable of shifts, but the signature was not like this, nor was the stamp. I am not sure. I am not sure if it is the same document. I think there were two sheets of paper, not one. It is not a complete document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were other dates on there. As you can see that particular document, Exhibit 361, refers to June and July, and the other documents refer to following dates, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you say so it must be that way. I just say that I have seen two sheets of paper. I do not know whether this was one of them. I do not remember. I did not pay any attention after that. I just think that it was signed by the Chief of Police, Simo Drljaca. The signature here is Jankovic Mile. I am not sure if this is the paper. If there is another paper I would kindly ask you to give me that paper so I can tell you for certainty whether we are talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this marked as Prosecution Exhibit 362.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a complete document. This is the form I received and you have here Chief of the Security Services Centre, Simo Drljaca, but I did not have this paper during my interview in Germany and my first interview in The Hague. I did have it at some point during a second interview. Mr. Wladimiroff who had asked one of your members if he could use that, gave me that document and then I had it. I saw the signature Simo Drljaca and I had a look at the document. I just skimmed it and I did not pay any attention to details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I ask that that document be tendered for admission, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 361 and 362?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because here under the paragraph 1 you see that here these are the extracts from timetable of shifts, and at that time we did not have the timetable of shifts available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ones which were introduced in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document is a compilation of those rosters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says here. I did not know whether it -- I did not know whether it was true or not, because here you have an extract from something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had that marked temporarily as two different Exhibits. I do not think that is appropriate under the circumstances. In addition I would like to have the witness shown this document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather 362, is that for other months, perhaps August and September?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. One is a letter -- those should be marked, it seems to me, 361A, B and C, and this would be C.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us see what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that part of the document as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, it is probably that it is, but I cannot claim with certainty when I saw it for the first time. This document is also an extract of something, of a timetable of shifts. So it is a copy of what was written in the police station in Prijedor. The signature is Marko Djinardja. I think that was the person who was Commander of the police station at that time. I was on duty. I was securing the police station in Prijedor and I was also in charge of securing the bus station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can submit the English translations at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is there any objection then to 361 becoming 361A, 362 will become 361B and what now has been marked for identification purposes will be 361C? Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection to the last Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then they will all be admitted as A, B and C 361.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you indicated that you do not recall referring to this document during the course of your interview with Mr. Reid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that I could use, I could refer to this document, but I do not remember whether I used it and in what way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall being asked a question about the allegations concerning the 20th, the time period on or around 20th July -- it is page 42 -- then being referred to the document by Mr. Wladimiroff, and then subsequently providing an answer that said: "In any case, I can say that that day I was on duty as a reserve traffic policeman in Orlovci. I was on duty from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m."? Is that something you did without recourse to the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. It is also possible that I had a look at the document. I think that his questions were put in such a way that I had to answer whether this was true. That is how I understood it. That was the kind of answer that I gave him, whether it was true or not. At first sight I realised it was not an official document. I knew that there were other documents which are kept in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I believe the question on page 41, Mr. Tadic, was: "Is there anything you wish to say in relation to that allegation?" Does such a general question refresh your memory about whether or not you referred to the document yourself in providing such a specific date and time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that these dates were not especially important in our interview, but it became clear at that moment that there were original documents at that time, and the investigator could go there and check those documents. I only thought that we could talk about whom I spoke and so on at that time. It is perfectly clear how I spent my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you wrote your work report in August 1993 and you did so at a time when you were preparing to leave Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not sure whether I was going to leave at that time. It occurred on the 9th, but I was not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By that time you were already aware of allegations against you concerning activities in camps and during the cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had read some information in Serbian paper Vrema. They were just general allegations in relation to crimes committed. That is what I read in Banja Luka. That information had been sent from Prijedor by the Prijedor authorities in agreement with some journalists, and that is how Mrs. Monika Gras arrived with some policemen to make a video of me in January '93. She could not come to Kozarac without the approval of Mr. Simo Drljaca who finally issued an approval for that, because he knew what he was doing. The subject of Omarska was then simply transferred to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You knew this letter was intended to be sent to the media in Yugoslavia and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That letter should be read from the beginning till the end, and you can easily see that it does not make sense. It relates to a period of three years. I was not a professional. I could not compose a professional letter for the media. That information was taken from the minutes that were available to me at that time. I was being persecuted. I was on the run and that is what I managed to write in a very short period of time. You have many mistakes there. You have very long periods of time. There is a mention of the date of 10th June and so on. So I put zero instead of six. It was not important for me at that moment. I did not think about that at that moment. The essence of what had happened was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You planned to take this letter with you to Germany where it was ultimately seized from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. A lot of documents that you have offered here as evidence against me were found with those papers. If I had thought about that I would have never taken them with me to Germany. I do not know what kind of use I could have with those documents in Germany, I mean, the fact that I had weapons and things like that. I was a persecuted man at that time, ever since the beginning of 1993 until my departure from Yugoslavia. I did not leave because I wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This letter was intended to be sent, not to remain in your personal confidential possession as a secret, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not think about that at all. I only remembered about this letter from when the German authorities told me about it. I did not think of any of the documents that I had. I packed within half an hour. I did not have a visa for Germany and it was by sheer luck that I got it through my brother. I left with the Yugoslav selection to Germany. My brother did not send me a guarantee. My brother did not want me to go to Germany and my wife was not there with my brother. She was staying with his former wife and I did not send my wife and my children to my brother's. I had a very bad experience with Serbs, whoever they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this letter, the work report, did you in fact send one copy off or deliver one copy off to somebody, or did you simply take it with you in your papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I wrote that letter I made two copies of it. One copy was delivered by me on the same day in Prijedor, and I took the other with me. I left it in my flat in Prijedor. At the time of my arrest on 9th August I just grabbed whatever I could get hold of and fled to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I appreciate that. To whom did you deliver the letter in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very entrance in to Prijedor there is a sort of reception office and I left it there. It is a common procedure if you wanted to hand over any kind of document, if you wanted your document to reach some authority.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. At the very entrance to what? You say "at the very entrance"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the town hall in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The Monika Gras interview with you which was made into a film, when did that occur, about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. I remember that event very well. On 31st December in '92 I was in Belgrade. I was there for the New Year's Eve. I came back and I was surprised to learn. At the beginning of '93 in January I went to my work, my work as the Secretary of the Local Commune in Kozarac, and all of a sudden I saw just across the church a TV team and Monika Gras, whose name I learned later on, were there together with two policemen from Prijedor. They were talking to Dusanka, I do not her surname but at that she was working as a teleographer (?) in the Prijedor police station. At one she said: "They are looking for you. They want to talk to you." I said: "Why to me?" They explained that they had come to Prijedor under somebody's instructions and the Commander had sent them there. I did not know what it was all about, and Dusanka told me: "They are talking about the church. They do not believe that it is 120 years old church", and so on. I told them that I did not want to talk to such people, because I did not know what the conversation would be about.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But I only wanted to know the date and you have told me that. One other thing I wanted to know about it. Did the film accuse you of acts similar to some of those in the present indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and partly the text and the warrant of arrest, that was publicly declared by Emin Jakupovic on TV and some other people. It was obviously a suggestion of Monika Gras. They kept saying "Dule, Dule, Dule". There was a big montage which showed my image at that time. They were filming me and I was not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I think that at one stage in your evidence you mentioned somebody by the name of Cirkin, and I think that you referred to him as having a criminal record. Am I right in the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is that the same person as the Captain Cirkin that we, long ago now, in evidence heard had been organising Muslim resistance, or is it a different person altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a different person. I now remember the name. His name was Ramiz Cirkin. He had spent many years in prison and he was well-known in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If it is a different person ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not the same person.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If it is not the same person I am not interested. The next thing I wanted to ask you was about the checkpoint at Orlovci. We have heard a lot about caravans, containers. You spoke about caravans. Initially there was nothing. Then there was a caravan. At any time were there two containers beside the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is quite possible. To be frank, I cannot say with certainty because we did not pay much attention to that vehicle. We never really used them. They belonged to the military police. They had their instructions about that. They did what they wanted with that. It is possible. We mainly used our vehicles, vehicles which belonged to the police, because we had a radio connection from the car.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The final question I wanted to ask you was, you said, I think, that the real reason for your frequent arrests by the military police in 1993 was not a question, as I had perhaps earlier gathered, of rivalry over the ownership of a cafe or the operation of a cafe in Prijedor, but there was another real reason. What was that real reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a very long time I thought that the cafe was the reason and my family thought so. However, when I publicly stated that I would not use that cafe, those business premises, I had adapted it and so on, but it would have been absurd for me to enter into any kind of business at that time because the military had the power at that time. But after several arrests took place I realised that that was not the case, because they knew that the cafe was no longer a problem. The real reason I think was the fact that I had become involved in the revival of Kozarac. They did not want Kozarac, life to be brought back to Kozarac, and they did everything they could not to revive that town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only later that I understood. The municipal Crisis Staff had an absolute power. They were above everyone else, above the Regional Crisis Staff and the area of Kozarac at that time was under the jurisdiction of the Regional Crisis Staff in Lamovita. We were just mocked by people from the Regional Crisis Staff. We were insignificant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Additional questions, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have a second. Thank you your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you mentioned that you intended to drop the letter off for a municipal official in Prijedor. Who was that official?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know with whom I left it. I did not think about that. I know that in the town hall there were some authorities like in any other town hall, but it was not any specific individual and I did not believe that it would end up in the hands of Karadzic, as you stated. If it had ended up in his hands I would not have been arrested maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said you went to Germany as part of the Yugoslav selection. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Yugoslav selection. My brother was very influential, a karate sportsman, and very often he was the host of the Yugoslav selection in karate in Germany. So he had intervened with the then President of the karate association and he asked him to help me with the visa, because I had no other opportunity to go to Germany. So I was some kind of -- I accompanied the selection, the karate selection of Yugoslavia at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question. Mr. Tadic you just indicated that you did not know the person whom you left the letter with at the reception centre. But who was the official to whom you wanted this letter delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any specific person in mind. I was just thinking of someone who could help me and who could check those data. I did not think about that. If I had thought about that I would have sent it maybe to the Chief of Police as any ordinary citizen would do. I did not have a clear idea in my mind about what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you left it with the reception centre in Prijedor, at the town hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you leave it in an envelope with anyone's name on it or did you just leave it with the receptionist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in an envelope. I just left it there. I put "Municipal" ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Municipal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- "Assembly Prijedor".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I presume will be excused. You will be with us. My usual question is, is there any objection to the witness being permanently excused. I am sure you have heard me say that for several months now. So I do not have to say that today. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10. I understand from Mr. Bos that you expect you will be finishing tomorrow with your case in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned until the following day).

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time)
(The Court adjourned for a short time)
